It drat became famous about Wired Collars.—Several doctors have expressed the the middle of the eighteenth century, when a Dr. opinion that the wired collars so modish nowadays are Russell, who resided there, induced this aristocracy to responsible for much in the way of headache. They believe in the benefits of sea bthing. It attracted advise us if wires or bones we must have, to place them many wealthy and titled people on this score,previously slantwise, and on no account to allow them to press to the time when George IV, as Prince of Wales, made upon a vein. Keenly alive as we are to the vast import- Brighton the most famous of south-coast watering ance of a well-boned collar, we are not likely to give places. The royal palace called the Marine Pavilion, ! up or to take to the slantwise ariangement,—which is now the property of the .tlywn, was built in 1784, but rarely a success—but we can one and all see to it that modern Brighton was then already in the making. Of ! the bones or wires are so placed as to avoid any pres- late years, it has suffered from the ever-increasing i numbers and attractions of newer health resorts, but sure upon veins. there are many like the Princess Royal who say they , : :•are never so well as when at Brighton. That is mainly why the Duke. of Fife keeps up his house there, where the King has been staying. It is two houses knocked into one, commanding fine sea views, and one of the houses of which it is part was bought by the Duke of Fife from Mr. John Corlett, well-known in sporting circles.

The resort of Fashion and Beauty.—Stevenson, who tried many places in search of health, stayed at Brighton, and refers to it in his book entitled "The Open Air." He praises the dry, clear, bracing atmosphere, and remarks that" there are more hand- some women in Brighton than an where else in the world." As to whether he was referring to residents or visitors, is not quite clear, but he was speaking of the fashionable season in the late autumn. He goes on to say that' good-looking women who would be admired in other places pass by without notice," and that remark would scarcely apply to the summer excursion season, when Brighton is over-run by cheap trippers from London. Keeping up Appearances.—One of the judges recently had some remarks to offer on the folly of " keeping up appearances." It has been said that "appearance" is everything, and that is about all that is demanded by our twentieth century civilisation, but it is no unworthy motive that impels people, who have fallen upon evil i days, to keep the fact as far as possible from the world. To what extent they can, they keep up appearances, , but there are others to whom the judge referred, who ; try to make a great show in the world, upon inadequate means. They live a life of pretence, always hopelessly in debt, but still they have their afternoons," their "at homes," and dinner parties, the astonishing thing , about them being the length of time they stave off the inevitable crash that is bound to come in the end. 1 Every one knows this class of people, and the mistake they make, but, if the whole body of judges were to ; discourse on the folly of trying to make a display on inadequate means, it would not appreciably reduce the numbers who are constantly endeavouring to do so. Women's First Claim to Old Age Pensions.—We hear a good deal about women's demands in these days, and Mother Shipton appears to have been right when she said that the twentieth century would be a century of women's progress. The demand for votes for women is now followed by the cry of pensions for women, and Canon Barnett suggests that as there is not money enough for all, women should come first, as having the greater claim to old age pensions. As a worker for wages, a woman earns much less than a man, and as a wife or widow she often has to keep the wolf from the door. There are sources of employment open to elderly men who have lived decent lives, but there are few posts open to the working woman who is past her strength and skill, with scrubbing brush and saucepan. In New Zealand it is found and acknow- ledged by the authorities that women are the far more worthy recipients of pensions. There are, of course, exceptions, but as a rule they are not to blame to the same extent as are men, for the poverty which over- takes them in old age. In numberless cases this is brought upon them by the faults of others, and more- over experience in New Zealand goes to show that the women spend their pensions much more creditably than do many of the men. The Queen Dowager of Portugal.—There have been few more pathetic figures in history than Queen Maria Pia,of Portugal. That ha a led some of the papers to speak of her as if she were old and infirm, but as a matter of fact she is the junior of Queen Alexandra by some three years, and is a very active woman. The only daughter of King Victor Emmanuel of Italy, she was married when very young, and the late King Carlos was born when his mother was only sixteen. She has lived to mourn husband, also brother, the late King Humbert of Italy. who was assassinated,and the same cruel fate has now robbed her of son and grandson, King Carlos, and the Crown Prince. Like the Empress Eugenie, she is truly a woman of many sorrows, and one of the most pathetic figures in Europe. Dangerous Wraps.—From a health point of view, the new half-season coats and wraps leave much to be desired. All, or nearly all, are considerably cue away at the neck, just meet over the bust, and from thence slope away again in the approved swallow-tail fashion. The dainty waistcoats worn with these wraps closely resemble a man's full-dress waitcoat, and therefore afford no protection to the neck and chest, which in nine cases out of evevy ten is quite inadequately covered with a very fascinating lingerie blouse. As we have yet to face the keenest month of the year, these new coats are likely to prove something of a delusion and a snare, but if modish we must he, our best plan is to provide ourselves with an underbodice of flannel or some other fabric capable of protecting our throat and chest from the searching spring winds. Mixing Colours.—Useful morning tailor-mades, are still built with the coat and skirt matching, but when more dressy toilettes are in question, the tailors are introducing little coats and wrens which differ from the skirts not only so far as the fabric is concerned, but the colour too. First came the little velvet coatees, matching exactly in colour the accompanying cloth skirt, now we have a coat of one colour, and a skirt of another, the two hues being in evidence in the hat and underskirt. The notion when well carried out, affords a welcome change, still, there is no denying the fact that it is a fashion more suitable for those women blessed with a good dress allowance. The " necessitons "would do better to remain faithfnl to one coiner, and one only as each spring comes round, ringing the changes by means of divers shades the chosen hue.
MADGE.

_ Gayer Clothes at Weddings.—Of late years guests seem to have grown more or !AM careless about wedding toilettes, anything seems to do, and if in mourning, they wear gloomy black trappings quite calmly, often without the smallest effort to lighten them in any way. A quarter of a century ago the woman who either could not or would not discard black garments for the occa- sion, stayed away from weddings, but nowadays a black toilette is often worn when the wearer has not the smallest need to so array herqelf. Consequently from a modistio point of view weddings have become quite uninteresting events, the sprinkling of smart gowns upon several recent occasions, having almost reached vanishing point. div.head: YOUR SKIN IN WINTER.
div.p: YOUR SKIN IN WINTER.

Cold, Raw Days bring Skin Troubles. • Few people can boast of a skin healthy and strong en ,ugh to resist the treacheries of these raw, cold days. The effect of the wind, rain, and frost is seen in rough, blotchy faces, chafed cheeks, chapped hands, pimply eruptions, and cold sores. One reason is that the skin in winter does not get enough ventilation, heavy clothing and indoor confinement choking or poisoning the pores. The natural oil baths usually got during perspiration, which are necessary to maintain a workable flexibility of the tissues, are now seldom obtained, and the blood circulation is impeded. As a con- sequence the skin becomes impoverished, ill- nourished, rough and scaly—an easy prey to disease germs or pois mous substances. There is one way in which Nature can be safely assisted—just when she asks for assistance—by a liberal application of Zam-Buk over the rough patches or nasty sores. Be as prompt in response to Nature's call for help as you know how, remembering that chronic ulcers are, in the first instance, simply a breakdown of tissue that has got below par. Dressings with Zam-Buk will speedily relieve, and finally cure, the worst skin disease. The herbal juices in Zam-Buk are indeed so potent that they will overoorne any contamination of the tissue that may have resulted from the use of course ointments, composed mainly of rancid animal fats. Proper moisture is ensured, and Zam-Buk induces the blood to circulate more freely near the surface, thus enabling the skin to get proper nourishment once more. Normal activity and strength are eventually restored, and in the end the skin is bound to become healthy, moist, velvet-like, and unaffected on the most wretched of days. In the most serious cases of long standing disease Zam-Buk is of inestimable value. That fierce farm of eczema which lies dormant during the summer and breaks out each winter or spring with agonising intensity may be permanently overcome by persevering with this powerful skin cure. Zam-Buk kills pain, allays irritation, takes out inflammation, expels disease, and finally grows new and healthy skin over the parts worn out by sores. In its composition Z im-Buk resembles the rich herbal balms used by the Greeks and Romans 2,000 years ago. It is the greatest healer known to modern science.

Mr. S. Illighouse, coroner, conducted the adjourned inguiry into the circumstances attending the death of William Glover, the six weeks old son of Arthur and Mary Glover, of 3, brackley-street, at the Police Station on Monday. The inquest had been adjourned from the previous Tuesday, in order that a post-mortem examination of the body of the deceased could be made. Dr. Smith, who made the post-mortem, stated that the weight of the body was exactly six pounds. There were no marks of violence on it. Internally there was a very fair amount of fat, showing that the child was well nourished. He was of the opinion that the child died from natural ceases, viz., convulsions. The Coroner said that on January Bth, 1907, an inquest was held on the body of Arthur Stanley Glover, son of the same parents. On that occasion Dr. Peacocke made the post-mortem examination, and found that death was due to tubercular disease of the mesenterie glands, and the jury returned a verdict accordingly. In that case the husband said his wife drank very heavily and neglected her home and children, and in conjunction with Inspector Cox, of the N.S.P.C.C., he had tried to mprove her, but it had been of no avail. However, that was nut a court of morals, and the jury had only to state what was the cause of death.

The jury returned a verdict in accordance with the medical evidence, and added that they thought the mother was deserving of censure. Inspector Cox, of the National Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Children, spoke to the woman having previously been sent to prison for three months for neglecting her children. Several people had done their best to try and reform her, but she would not take any notice of the warnings. The Coroner said to the husband that, unless his wife improved, the best course would be for him to apply to the magistrates for a separation on the grounds of her being a habitual drunkard, and the magistrates then had power to order her removal to an inebriates' home. Addressing the mother, Mr. Brighouse said :—This is your last chance. My advice to you is to give up drink. I know what I should do if I were your husband. I should deal with you in a different way than he does. I would cure you before this week was out. (To the husband) : you give here good hammering. Never mind the magistrates convicting you of assault. The Husband : She will give me one. The Coroner : If you cannot do it, send for me. I will straighten her up. Kind words are absolutely wasted on her.

div.head: DRESS-FASHION-HOME.
div.p: DRESS-FASHION-HOME.
LACE WAISTCOATS.

Lace waistcoats made to fit tightly, buttoning with four paste buttons in front, and lined with white satin, will be seen in great numbers during the season, says a fashion writer. They are in all materials, from the most elaborate to the simplest. One sees them in brocaded velvet, in embroidered satin, in exquisite lace over satin, in printed velvet, and in inexpensive white or cream materials with appliques of cretonne. The buttons are few. They are chiefly rather small and toned to suit the colours of the waist- coat itself. After the blousincss of blouses these neatly-fitting little garments are much appreciated. ,

div.head: USEFUL PINAFORE.
div.p: A USEFUL PINAFORE.

Our sketch illustrates a pretty and most .use- ful pinafore, suitable for a girl of from two to twelve years of age. It may be successfully realised in almost any kind of washing fabric, such as linen, cambric, lawn, cotton, muslin, zephyr, or print, and is just the thing for every- day nursery wear. The upper part of the pina- fore consists of a square yoke which is machined all round the edges, and is finished at the tpp by

a little frill of Valenciennes lace. On to this yoke the fulness of the material is set in a succession of short tucks, the bottom of the pinafore being finished by a wide hem. The sleeves consist of short frills of the material finished with an edg- ing of the Valenciennes lace; but, if liked, the same design may be carried out without the sleeve, and with a simple frill round the armhole.

div.head: TYRANNY OF EHE FEATHER BOA.
div.p: THE TYRANNY OF EHE FEATHER BOA.

Spring is in the air, cold as the air is. Some people are even thinking of discarding their furs. While there is yet time, may one entreat the makers of neckwear to lighten the tyranny of the feather boa? "All Englishwomen wear feather boas," says the foreigner, and smiles. One feels rather indignant at that smile, remarks the Lady, but one has to acknowledge the truth of the statement which preceded it. We have emancipated ourselves from so many conven- tions that it seems all the more strange that we should meekly put our necks under the yoke of the feather boa summer after summer. Clothe our necks in some other fashion," should be the special prayer to the gods of millinery now that spring is approaching. I have no animus against the feather boa "per so" and at its best, but things grown common do lose their dearest at- tractions, and it does not suit everyone to have the space between the line of shoulder and line of chin entirely blocked by a ruffle of barn-door feathers.

div.head: CHARMING GOWN.
div.p: A CHARMING GOWN.

One of the most noticeable features of the new gowns is the rapid increase in favour of crossover styles, which bid fair to supplant the long-popular pinafore effects as spring advances. The charming model pictured in our sketch is particularly graceful and becoming, the alliance of Princess and tunic styles being quite the latest thing in the fashionable world. The oricr'i- nal was carried out in thin light faced cloth ofa charming shade of marron brown. Fitting closely over the shoulders. where is is finished with modified Mandarin sleeves, the corsage is

draped round the figure in most becoming fashion, the drapery being drawn round to the left side, where it fastens with five large black satin buttons embroidered in much-tarnished gold thread. Inside the crossover corsage is a smart little shaped vest of black satin, em- broidered with a simple design worked in the tarnished-gold thread. Above this vest come two inner crossovers, the first of marron-brown vel- vet adorned with the embroidered buttons, the second of imitation Irish guipure. Inside again comes a dainty little chemisette of tucked white net or tulle. The tunic is opened up the left side, and falls in very graceful folds from the hips, displaying a considerable amount of under- I skirt on the left side, and but the merest suspi- cion on the right.

div.head: GOOD LOT OF THE NORWEGIAN' GIRL.
div.p: THE GOOD LOT OF THE NORWEGIAN' GIRL.

In the present workaday world probably, of all the nations, the Norwegian girl has the best of it, declares "Lady Phyllis" in the Bystander. She is trained to a profession almost as infallibly as her brothers, trained also to take it seriously, yet naturally, very unlike the view that it is the last resort of the unfortunate which is so often the aspect of an Englishwoman. Norwegian girls are well educated, and the most independent women in Europe; frank, fearless, without re- straint, they find less hardships in following a business life than some of the well-protected hot. house plants of English womanhood. They are ahead of American girls, inasmuch as they have never been spoilt with superfluous fortunes, and though travel is considered., whenever possible, a necessary finish to education, they have, happily, never degenerated into the mere sightseer like our cousins across the Atlantic. TO-DAY'S RECIPE.

APPLE MERINGUE PlE—Cook three pints of good cooking apples with one small cupful of water. adding when done the juice and half the grated peel of a lemon, one tablespoonful of butter, and two-thirds of a cupful of sugar. Stand away to cool, add then the beaten yolks of three eggs, and pour into a deep pie-pan lined with rich pastry and bake. When done, cover with the beaten whites of the eggs, sweetened with powdered sugar. and brown slightly in the oven. No apple that will not readily cook to a soft pulp on top of the stove should ho put into any made dish. The best of all zN-)plie-pies is made of uncooked apples cut into eighths, then sprinkled well with ',agar, dusted with allspice—toe nest ot 441 flav- ourings for apple-pies—and generously dotted with butter. It is well to mix a little tiowr with the sugarif 'the apples are very juicy.,

div.head: SCIENCE NOTES AND NEWS.
div.p: SCIENCE NOTES AND NEWS.

NEW THEORY ABOUT METEORITES. According to a prominent official engaged in astronomical work for the Governmont at Washington, some of the meteorites that fall vim the earth possess a peculiar structure, indicating that they have been more than once in a molten condition. He concludes that they came originally from a volcano situ- ated in some distant part of space,, but that before reaching the earth they were subjected to great heat which metamorphosed their structure. He suggests that they may have passed through the atmosphere of a sun, or may have been fused through the sudden birth of a new and neighbouring star.

RADIUM AND BIRTHMARKS. Professor Fournier has been investigating remarkable theory put forward some time ago by Dr. Wickham, a well-known physician of Paris, on the treatment of "wine stains" (birthmarks) by radium. In a report to the Medical Academy, the professor says he has come to the conclusion that the stains disap- pear after applications of flat discs, covered by a special varnish, into which a salt of radium is incorporated. " Angiomes," or superficial tumours, even of great size,, under ' the influence of the radium rays, thew pro- gressive diminution, arriving eventually at a complete levelling. The repaired tissues are supple, resume their normal colour, and have the appearance of healthy skin. The appli- cations of the radium are quite painless.

A TEST FOR DIAMONDS. Even pawnbrokers have often been taken in by preciousstone fakers. There are, how- ever, a few simple tests which will consider- ably aid a buyer of diamonds. One test is to prick a needle hole through a card and look at the hole through the doubtful stone. If the latter is spurious, two holes will be seen, but if it is a diamond only one hole will be visible. This is a delicate test, because it is difficult to see even a sharp and defined ob- ject through a diamond. Another test is this: If the finger is placed behind and viewed through the stone with a watchmaker's glass, the grain of the akin will be plainly seen if the stone is not a diamond. But if it is to, diamond the grain of the skin will not be dis- tinguished at all.

YERTICAL CURRENTS AND FOHN WINDS , In the course of a trip across the Channel in her balloon, Mrs. Harbord experienced a strong vertical current which made the bal- loon shoot up very rapidly. Afterwards it was caught in a downward vertical current, and fell with great speed. The occurrence of such vertical currents of air probably gives , the key, says the Globe, for the explanation of those remarkable breezes known as Fan winds. The name was first given to certain warm winds blowing down from the snow and ice-covered mountains in Switzerland, and producing extensive thaws. Such a downward current as that met with in the recent bal- loon voyage impinging on a mountain summit would be warmed by compression, and flow down the mountain side as a warm breeze. The downward movement might even be one of warmer air from a higher level.

div.head: FOHN WIND IN THE ARCTIC.
div.p: FOHN WIND IN THE ARCTIC.

The term Fan is also applied to similar , warm breezes from cold mountains in other countries. In North America, however, where such a wind blows down from the Rockies, it is known as the Chinook. The effect of the Fohn is most striking when it occurs in the Arctic regions. There sometimes in mid-win- ter such a wind will blow for several days, and produce extensive thaws. In Greenland a Fan wind from the snow-covered interior may render for a day or two that bleak and desolate land warmer than the South of ! France, though it is still wrapped in winter darkness.

div.head: MIGHTY WORK OF EARTHQUAKES.
div.p: MIGHTY WORK OF EARTHQUAKES.

Dr. John M. Clarke, from studies of re- cords and contemporary documents combined with that of geological dislocations in the St. Lawrence and Champlain Valleys, concludes that the Canadian earthquake of 1663 was the severest disturbance the Western Continent has ever suffered from terrestrial dislocation. There was a great movement of the crust along the course of the St. Lawrence River, the paleozoic rocks slipping against the shield of crystalline rocks where they are in contact, and the destructive effects from Montreal down to Tadousac were tremendous. Dr. Clarke thinks that the displacement of the rocks was continued in the direction of the Lake Champlain Valley along the line of con- tact with the great crystalline mass of the Adirondack region.

div.head: BOTTOM OF THE OCEAN.
div.p: THE BOTTOM OF THE OCEAN.

To an enormous extent, the bed of the ocean is covered with lava and pumice-stone. Still more remarkable is it to find the floor of the ocean covered in many parts with the dust of meteorites. These bodies whirl about in the heavens like miniature comets, and are, for the most part, broken into innumer- able fragments. We are all familiar with these heavenly visitants as shooting-stars; but it has been only lately discovered that this cosmic dust forms layers at the bottotn of the deepest seas. Between Honolulu and Tahiti, at a depth of 2,350 fathoms—over two miles and a-half—a vast layer of this material exists. Falling upon land, this impalpable dust is (Indistinguishable; but accumulating for centuries in the sea depths, it forms a wondrous story of the continuous bombard- /neat of this planet by cometary bodies.

div.head: HOW OLD IS NIAGARA?
div.p: HOW OLD IS NIAGARA?

This question, always interesting for the light it throws on the past history of the earth, has had many answers. Dr. J. W. Spencer, from studies on the spot, finds that the mean rate of recession of the falls at pre- sent is 4.2 ft. per year, and that this has been the rate for approximately 227 years. But owing to the fact that originally the waters of Lake Erie only were discharged over the falls, giving but one-fifteenth of the present water supply, the rate of recession was at first much slower. A sudden widening of the gorge above Foster's Flat indicates the posi- tion of the falls when the other Great Lakes began to discharge into Lake Erie. From his data, Dr. Spencer calculates the entire age of the falls at 39,000 years. The cutting, with the full power of the four lakes, is esti- mated to have lasted 3,500 years.

CROCODILE AND SLEEPING SICKNESS. As a result of his investigations of the sleeping sickness the famous German savant, Dr. Koch, concludes that the crocodile plays an important part in the spread of this dread disease. In order to stamp out the plague, he declares that the crocodile must be exterminated. The infection of the sleep- ing sickness is carried by a species of glos• sine, or tsetse fly, and Dr. Koch believes i:•at this insect lives exclusively on the blood of the crocodile. If the latter were exter- minated the fly would be deprived of its foon supply, and become extinct. From a natural history point of view the destruction of :o interesting and characteristic an African animal as the crocodile would be a regret- table incident, says the Globe, which questions whether it would have the desired result. The very fact that these flies suck human blood seems to shew that they are not exclu- sively confined to that of the crocodile. And might it not be that in the absence of the latter they would bite men more frequently? Or, as crocodiles got scarcer, a taste for other hosts might be evolved.

div.head: MUSCLES OF THE ARM.
div.p: THE MUSCLES OF THE ARM.

If the muscles in the arm of the average man were put together and a nervous impulee passed into them, their contraction would lift a weight of 2241 h. from the ground. Muscles have the unique power, when stimulated by nerve impulse. pf contracting. somewhat as runner bands might do if they coma syleeze themselves up shorter. They are, in fact, the reverse of rubber; for they contract only and cannot stretch out.

div.head: rALL RIGHTS RESERVED. I THE UNDERSTUDY
div.p: rALL RIGHTS RESERVED. I THE UNDERSTUDY
•BY HERBERT RUSSELL, Author of "True Blue," "The Longshoreman," "Elmira," "The Slump in Le Rois," "The Burning Sea," "The Picaroon," &e.

"It's a great nuisance—no end of a nuisance!" said the stage manager, meditatively stroking his blue chin. "Our leading lady is a tower of strength to an otherwise weak cast. Without her the shew will be about as brilliant as a Scotch fit-up!" And he once again frowned over the lines of the little missive in which Miss Bertha Gilroy announced that, having "turned over" her ankle in crossing the road, she could not possibly take her part that night as the erring daughter in "A Father's Remorse."

"There is only one thing to be done," said the fur-coated gentleman who "worked the front of the house,' tapping a cigarette upon his thumb- nail. "We must make the best of a bad job, and put the understudy on." _
"No other way out of it, I suppose," com- plained the stage manager, with an aggrieved air. "Kitty Lamb is a charming little girl, but--"
"Not strong enough for the part, eh I' " - -

"Ab-so-lutely futile, I'm afraid, dear boy! Still, we must give her a chance. I will call a rehearsal for this afternoon—pretty sharp work ! Get your printing out as soon as you can, and give the Press a hint to-night to be as kind to us as possible, for some of the provincial youngsters like to shew their smartness by jumping on you, and business is none too good. Ha! hero comes little Lamb now."

When Kitty Lamb was informed, in brusque but not unkindly terms, that she was to do the erring daughter that night, a dual emotion of joy and fear took possession of her. Joy at the opportunity to rise out of the subordinate back- ground of her own role; fear that in comparison with the stately, massive, and distinctly raucous Bertha Gilroy, her own slim stage presence and refined mannerism would form a contrast dis- tasteful to her audience. The company had been but three weeks on tour, and Kitty Lamb was the cognomen of a girl who was as yet a 'prentice- hand to the stage, to which calling she had turned in the hour of stress, to try and support life and an invalid mother on one-twelve-six a week.

"You'll do your best, dear," said the stage manager, addressing her in the customary vernacular of behind the scenes. "You'll see by the call-board that there's a rehearsal at three. I've sent round to the crowd to get 'em together, and I'm sure dear old dada will play up to you for all he's worth, to try and pull you through all right. Throw yourself right into the part, kiddy; don't think of your audience; don't think of anything but delivering your lines as effectively as possible; and, above all, don't be nervous.

"It will mean a good deal to me if I should do pretty well ? " she said, half abstractedly, for her thoughts just then were far away in a little home that could be rendered so much the brighter and more cheerful if her salary were but a pound a week more.

"It may mean the beginning of fame, wealth, and swollen head," answered the stage manager. "So wire in at once, dear, and read up the part as hard a you can." He turned away, muttering under his breath: "Why on earth they ever took on such a stripling as understudy to the buxom Gilroy, I'm blesst if I know! "

The editor of the Daily Herald was decidedly glum. The case-room and the reporter's room were in conspiracy against his peace of mind. Yes—it was no use talking, because he was perfectly convinced about the matter, and so there was an end of it. "Fourteen literals in one column of minion !" he hissed, smacking down a copy of that morning's town edition. "And Alderman Smudge is reported to be in favour of the pollution antidote scheme, when every schoolboy in the place knows that he nearly died of a fit of apoplexy brought on by his frenzied attack upon Councillor Jobling's ridiculous proposals. Bah! Jiggered if I know what the staff of this office is coming to!" With which conjecture, hazarded on an average twenty times a day, he snatched off his spectacles and vented his nervous energy upon the misty pebbles with the aid of one of the Daily Herald's gaudy Jubilee commemoration handkerchiefs.
A kurock at the door, and the chief reporter dawned upon the editor's gaze. "Well, what now, Mr. Lyne ?"- „__ . . . . .

"Mr. Rertram has just sent down a note by his wife' sir, to say that as he's confined to his room witha bad attack of neuralgia, he cannot carry out his engagements to-day." "Humph! Strange how neuralgia seems to run in his family. What's he marked for in the engagement diary ? " -'To cover a meeting of the Town Council, to write up a descriptive column of the unveiling of Sir Timothy Tate's statue, to do a good breezy introduction to that story of shipwreck which came from our Hull correspondent, to sum- marise the vaccination statistics for the last seventeen years, to help in general sub-editing, and to do a notice of the Royalty Theatre to-night." "Well, how about it, Mr. Lyne ? " "I think I can get all the rest of the work done, sir, if you can just put a man on to do the Theatre. I'm told it's rather a special show there this week; they've increased their adver- tising, and will expect an adequate notice." "Humph! Who can we put on to do it?" "There's only young Hallowes available' sir, and I should not definitely like to say that he is man enough for the job." "Send him in to me."
The chief reporter vanished, and a tall, clean- shaven youth of about five-and-twenty entered the room.

"Mr. Hallowes, I want you to try your hand on a theatre notice to-night. There's a new pro- duction coming to the Royalty, so do, your best. Not had any experience in this sort of work—now, pray don't start making difficulties. Just try and write out your impressions in an intelligent form—that's all you've got to do. Don't merely summarise the programme and call that a criticism, and don't do as that young ass of a Redfern did when writing a notice of "Hamlet" the other day: fill up half a column with a dis- quisition upon the defects of Shakespeare's con- struction viewed by the light of modern methods. Just write up about four or five sticks of stuff, telling the story of the new show in a pithy manner, with a few shrewd comments upon the acting. That will do, Mr. Hallowes. I think you understand just what I want."

For the next -hour the ingenious youth buried his nose in back files of the Daily Herald, diligently reading up past theatrical notices, "so as to get the hang of how these things are done in our blooming rag!" as he explained to the sporting sub-editor, who wondered much to see HaHowes so studious.

...... There was a general indefinable air of depres- sion about the interior of the Royalty when the curtain rang up on the opening act of "A Father's Remorse." Notwithstanding the large element of "Monday night paper," the house was a particularly thin one, a circumstance which called forth many satiric pleasantries from the fur-coated gentlemen in front at the expense of the inhabitants of the place. The perfornuinPe was a melodrama of the stereotyped pea-green order, slightly overburthened with axiomatic morality, and passaged by transpontine curtains. The heavy lead knew his lines most imper- fectly, and the light comedy man missed his entry twice, forcing the remorseful father into laborious "gagging." The scenery, which was I very fair in itself, was atrociously set, the result of a heated altercation between the stage manager and the carpenter. The audience was distinctly lukewarm, with the exception of one !Calf- , inebriated occupant of the gallery. TEMPTING RHEUMATISM.
A winter foe readily contracted during
outdoor work or recreation. This cure by Dr Williams' Pink Pills is of speciol importance to men.

Although the unhappy experience of Rheumatism recorded below by young Mr DENTON, of 25, Markham- Street, Blackburn, may appear to concern only the crowds who watch football matches regardless of rain, hail or snow, the incident is of equal importahce to all whose work exposes them to winter weather. Damp clothes and wet boots are a source of danger to workers, often leading to Rheumatism, Chills, Sciatica, Lung or Kidney Troubles. A wet afternoon on a football ground led to acute Rheumatism in Mr. Denton's case, whose sufferings were intense until he found a splendid cure in Dr. Williams' Pink Pills.

div.head: 'aught Cold, followed by Rheumatism.
div.p: 'aught Cold, followed by Rheumatism.

I"David is very fond of football," said Mrs. Denton indulgently, " and be attends many matches. Last winter on one occasion he caught a severe cold,which I was soon followed by Acute Rheumatism, He has always been rather weak on the chest ; so it didn't surprise me when after one spell of cold and damp, lhe was seized with Rheumatism. The attack came so sharp and sudden that my son actually collapsed while at work, and he had to be carried home from the mill by his father. "He had to take to his bed sharp, with his ankles greatly swelled, and with agonising Rheumatic pains flying through his legs and feet. Worn away by pain he lost flesh rapidly,and his appetite quite failed him. div.p: The Examiner, Saturday, February 22, 1908
rat RIGHTS RESZETRD.,
THREE PHASES.
By THOMAS COBB.
Author of "The Friendships of Veronica,* "The Intriguers," "The Composite Lady,", "The Dissemblers," "Scruples," "Mr. Pup- ingham." ttc.

When I saw Freda coming along the High- street of our sedate country town, I wondered whether she would stop for a moment as she sometimes did, and speak a few words, thus marking a red letter day in my calendar. She walked on the sunny side of the way as was only fitting, wearing a light-coloured dress, tall, lithesome, with a pervasive cheerfulness and graciousness too tranquil to be gay. Yes, sh 3 was going to stop, and she held out her hand, looking lovelier :han I had ever seen her. "I was going to write to you," she said. " Won't you write still? " I asked. " Indeed, I am far too busy to waste my time now that we have met," she answered. "I wanted to know whether you can come to dine with us on Friday." "To dine!" "A quite astonishing event, isn't it?" cried Freda. "But we shall have another visitor," and I wondered why she blushed so charmingly. • Although I had known her people since they first came to the town three years before, this was the only occasion of their inviting me to a meal at the house. Her father had retired from one of the Government offices on a pen- • sion, her mother was a confirmed invalid, her brothers and sisters were uninteresting—but not ,to Freda. Upon her they seemed to depend for everything, and it was obvious that all their resources were taxed to maintain even a moderate appearance. From the outset the evening proved an un- comfortable one for me, though, I believe, for I nobody else. It was annoying to find myself the ' only person in morning clothes; but it appeat ed evident that they had all made the most of themselves for the occasion and for Rupert Sutcliffe.

He was a young man, twenty-five years of age, perhaps, with smooth, fair hair, parted very definitely down the middle, a thin, hatchet- shaped face, and prominent ears. Yet he was not ill-looking, and at least he was perfectly easy to "place." Sutcliffe was one of the golden youth of the period, his evening clothes were consummate, he had a slow, drawling voice, and he scarcely tried to disguise his bore- dom except when he spoke to Freda. The situation seemed easy to gauge, the only difficulty being to imagine where she had met a man so alien to her customary surroundings. He talked of horses, and comic operas, while Mr. Norton made ludicrous efforts to appear Interested. Myself Sutcliffe merely ignored, and I confess to a painful consciousness of shortcoming at least in the matter of apparel. After yawning a great deal during the last half- hour in the stiff drawing-room, Sutcliffe left at half-past ten. "Always pleased to see you at any time," said Mr. Norton as they shook hands. "Mr. Sutcliffe has promised to send me a toy-terrier puppy, father," cried Freda. I thought I would drive over with it to- morrow morning, don't you know," he answered; and when we were alone I gathered that she had met him at a local dance a few sveeks ago. "Mr. Sutcliffe is a young man to be envied," Mr. Norton explained. He has lately in- herited an immense fortune. He has a house in Berkeley-square, a shooting-box in Perth- shire, as well as a magnificent place near St. Albans." It was about a month later that I met Freda alone in the town, and once more, of her own initiative, she stopped and held out her hand. I suppose she was as intimate with me as with anybody in the neighbourhood. "I don't know whether I ought to be the one to tell you the news !" she cried, with charming self-consciousness.
"Suppose I guess?" I suggested. "Oh, you could never—"

"You 'receive my congratulations?" "I think I should like everybody to wish me well to-day," she answered, happily. "And I feel—you understand—as if I wished well to everybody. Of course," she added, "you have met Rupert." "Is the wedding to take place soon?" I asked.
"Dreadfully soon," she cried. "We aro actually to be married in a month. You must coma—you understand?"

In de course I received and accepted an in- citation. Mr. Norton had hired the local hall for the reception, and, for once in a way, ignored the question of expense. Many of the more important neighbours were invited, to- gether with a crowd of Sutcliffe's friends, who certainly lent an air of gaiety and festivity to the scene.
I suppose that no bride ever set forth on her honeymoon more happily.

Two years passed before I saw Freda again. During that time she had not come home, although Mrs. Norton and her brothers and sisters, in turns, had gone to visit her. I heard enthusiastic accounts of her new grandeur, and often speculated as to how she stood the great revolution in her circumstances. Then, to my surprise, I received an invitation to spend a week at Mrs. Sutcliffe's country house, and, after a little hesitation, this was accepted. Still, I set out by no means free from misgiving, being entirely unaccustomed to the kind of society which, doubtless, I should meet. I had never stayed at a large country house before, but yet Freda succeeded in setting me at ease before I had been ten minutes in the hall. About a dozen persons were there at afternoon tea; the ball resounded with laughter and somewhat loud voices, but of all the women Freda was unmis- takably queen.. She brought her husband to speak to me, although he seemed to have very little to say, and the next morning she insisted on introducing me to his heir—at that time thirteen months old.

"I need not ask whether all that rice which was showered upon you last time we met brought /tick?" I suggested. She turned with the brightest of faces. "I wonder why I have been so fortunate!" she cried. "Because sometimes, when I think of it, chance seems to have played such a large pert. You know I was invited to a dance by some people who were almost strangers, and mother didn't wish me to go because of the expense of a dress. If I hadn't gained my own way I should never have met Rupert." "An inconceivable proposition!" "Well, it is," she answered, with a laugh. During the week of my visit there was a con- stantly changing stream of guests. There were horses for them to ride if they had not brought their own, there were motor-ears and everything on the most lavish scale for their entertainment. Some of the guests Were eminent; all, save my- self, seemed to be distinguished by beauty, cleverness, or great possessions. Yet none of them was more beautiful than Freda, who moved amongst them all as if she had been to the manner born—witty, light-hearted, happy, and without a cloud visible in her sky. For my own part, I felt like a fish out of water, never having had the chance of shooting before, and being quite unable to risk the losses at bridge which others seemed to take as a matter of course.
Still, Freda made amends for every draw- back. She would talk by the half-hour about old days at home, and inquire after the staid people of the town just as if she still belonged to that world.
"I am immensely glad you were able to Come," she said on my last morning. "It was nice of you to remember an old iriend," I returned.
"Before long you must come again," were fier parting words.

But two months later I re2cived the offer of an appointment which would take me abroad for a few years, and during the whole of that time I heard no word concerning Freda. None Of DIY own friends were known to her, so that I

returnee o ngiana wrzn me natural supposi- tion that she still divided her time between the house in Berkeley-square, the shooting-box in Perthshire, and the place near St. Albans. Having no settled habitation I put up at a London hotel, and on the first Saturday deter- mined to run down to Brighton for a few days. A gale blew on Sunday from the south-west, and the Front, being far from a pleasant place to walk, wanting exercise in the afternoon, I turned my steps in the direction of Hove. The neighbourhood was new to me, and after passing the Town Hall I took one of the turn- ings to the right. scarcely heediniz my direction. in tact, until presently I recognised a oame. It was a road of small houses, rented perhaps at forty-five pounds a year. and one particular house had a rather large brass plats on its gate-post, with this inscription: "Mrs. Sutcliffe, Kindergarten."

The name gave a more definite direction to my thoughts, not that, at first, I for a moment associated it with Freda. But as I passed the house I was startled almost to read its name, painted in gold characters on the glass over the front door, "St. Albans." The coincidence clung to my mind, even after I had returned to the hotel. While nothing seemed much more unlikely than the supposition that the keeper of the kindergarten could have any connection with Freda, yet it appeared somewhat odd that a woman of her name should be living in a house called St. Albans. The coincidence made such an impression

on me that I rose before anyone else from dinner, put on my hat and overcoat, lighted a cigar, and once more set forth towards Hove. With some trepidation I rang the bell, deter- mined to ask to see Mrs. Sutcliffe just to satisfy my mind, and, on finding it was not Freda— (as how could it be?)—to make the best excuse I might for the intrusion. It was past nine o'clock on a windy Sunday evening, and the wide street was deserted. There was a light shewing between the laths of the venetian blind in the front room, another over the hall door, but for a time no one answered my ring. After waiting a decent interval I rang a second time, and a few moments later heard light steps in the hall. The next instant the door opened, and I stood face to face with Freda. Four years had passed since I parted from her the morning I quitted St. Albans, and she must now have been in her twenty-fifth year. She wore a simple, dark dress, which shewed to excellent advantage her slender, graceful figure. Her face, it is true, looked somewhat pale, but, still, she greeted me, after the first shock of surprise, with a reminiscence of her old cheerful smile. She began to speak rapidly: "I am sorry you had to ring twice," she said. "But I was putting my boy to bed, and the servant goes out on Sunday evening. Won't you come in?" she added, and I entered the hall, scarcely know- ing whether I was standing on my head or my heels. She led the way into the dining-room, where a cloth arranged for supper covered half the table, and then she indicated a chair. "If you haven't finished upstairs I can wait," I suggested. .. "Oh, yes, Rupert is asleep now," she answered. "I never leave him until he is asleep, and to-night he was a little fretful. How," she inquired, "did you discover me?" and I explained the chance which had brought us together again. Her face, far more beautiful, if that were possible, in maturity than it had been in girl- hood, possessed all, or nearly all, its former tranquillity. Whilst everyone of us has now and then to bow to fate, Freda, it appeared, bowed and smiled as well. "Of course," she said, " COU are full of curiosity to learn the cause of my migration. I am afraid we—soy hushand and I—were rather reckless. I seemed to have the idea that his income was without limit. His racing stable ruined him. We were compelled to give up every thing, and I—l came here." "And—SutclifTe?" I suggested. "Oh, you cannot imagine Rupert amidst such surroundings," she exclaimed. I saw that the room was extremely barely furnished. There was not a picture of any kind on the walls; only one gas burner was alight, and, although the night was cold, the fire had been allowed to burn out. ' "I cannot imagine him voluntarily absent from you," I returned, perhaps too bluntly. "Ah, well," she said, " it may be a question as to what is voluntary and what is in. voluntary." f "Where is he?" I demanded. 1 The next instant I felt sorry, when Freda 1 rose and stood with her back towards me as if to re-arrange something on the mantelshelf. 7 "He doesn't write to you?" I nevertheless I persisted. '"Rupert was always the worst of letter- writers, ' she answered. "Then you live here entirely alone?" " Alone!" she exclaimed, reproachfully. , "Why, I have my boy. He is the sweetest 1 little fellow—he will soon be six years of age. You understand that I had to think of his education—" "But why," I asked, "didn't you go to your father?" She shook her head slowly. "I was per- mitted to keep a few of my personal belongings when the others were taken," she explained, "and then I found this house. It is very pleasantly situated, you would say, if you saw it by daylight. I sold what I possessed and bought furniture at sales, then I invested in a brass plate. I assure you I feel immensely proud of my brass plate. First I got one small boy, then a little girl, and now I have twelve besides Rupert." "A poor living!" I remarked. "But imagine how good for him to have all those companions," she answered. "Besides, they keep me busy from morning until exening, , because when we're not at work I take them all I out. You would laugh to see us walking two by two. There is generally a competition to keep by my side. That is the reward for good conduct." "Upon my soul," I could not help exclaim-. ing, "it is difficult to imagine one more to be envied." She seemed to gaze at me with astonishment for a second, and then she said: "You have told me nothing about yourself." "Nothing to tell," I returned. "You are not married?" "No," I muttered. "How is it you have never married?" I forced a laugh as I held out my hand. "I must shew you out," she cried, and I followed her through the dim, narrow hall to the front door. Turning to shut the gate I looked at her again as she stood on the threshold, the bravest,, the most indomitable heart I baTe known. Ursa Em4.l -. PADGATE.

CHRIST CHURCH.—The incandescent lights which have been installed in this church were used for the first time on Sunday evening. The gas standards have been removed from the pews and have been utilized as pendants from the beams by inverting them. The work has been satisfactorily performed by the gas depart- ment of the Warrington Corporation. In addition to the lighting, Sunday also saw the completion of the overhauling and cleaning of the organ, which has been going on for nearly three weeks by Messrs. Wadsworth Bros. of Manchester. It may be interesting to recall the fact that the instrument was Wadsworth's exhibit, at the Jubilee Exhibition Manchester in 1887, and was purchased by the wardens of Padgate Church. Although not one of the larger organs, it is suitable for the size of the church, and the voicing of the pipes is particu- larly good.

1 Penny Popular Concerts. The attendance at the popular concert in Bold- street Schools on Saturday evening was a record for this season, no few than 1,100 persons being present; and considerably over 100 were unable to obtain ladmission. An excerlent programme of refined humour was provided by "The Sonnetts," a high class Liverpool Pierrot Company. Songs (humorous and otherwise), duets, and choruses were given by the troupe, and the audience were loud in their praises of Ithe entertainment. The Rev. T. Miller presided, and during the interval referred to the evils of drinking • and gambling.

div.head: NURSING ASSOCIATION. -- Thanking the Mayor.
div.p: NURSING ASSOCIATION. -- Thanking the Mayor.

A special meeting of the subscribers and friends of the Warrington and District Nursing Association was held on Wednesday evening for tha purpose of publicly thanking the Mayor for the splendid effort he had made in raising £3OO during the past two months to pay a debt to the bank and placing the Association in a sound financial position. The Rev. J. Yonge presided and was supported by the Mayor, Mr. J. D. Fairclongh and the Rev. C. Harvey Cook. Mr. FAIRCLOUGH read letters of apology for non- attendance from Mrs.C. Broadhurst, Mrs. G4ruett. Mrs. , Rylands,Messrs. G. Walker, F.Monks, F. W. Mooks,W. P.Rylands, J. Fairclough, T. Wadsworth,and Councillor Nield. The Mayort then read the list of donations which was as follows : £2O: Messrs. Ziba Armitage, J. J. , Bleckley, W.H.Bleckley,Col.Buckt on. J. M.Edel sten,W.J. Forshaw, Greene!! Whitley and Co., W.Long, F. Monks, , I F.W. Monks, C.E. Parker, Henry Roberts, W.P.Rylands, P. Walker and Sons, and J. Smethurst. Messrs. .LT. and T. Locker £5, J. Richardson, £5, F. R. Roberts £3 25., J. Fulton Smith £5. J. Allison £2 25., R. Dobson £1 Is. V. B. Davies £5, Warrington Wire Ropery £5, R. Chad- wick £2, J. A. Rushworth £3 35., Colonel Edelsten £4, W. B. Roberts,£s 55., S.Wakefield £s,Grosvenor (yearly ' subscription) 10s. 6d. and Mrs. J. Faircloug,h £5, which made the handsome total of £356 4s. 6d. (Applause.) The Rev. C. HARVEY COOK said that £356 4s. 6d. was a tangible expression of the Mayor's sympathy with that worthy institution the Warrington Nursing Association and be (Mr. Cook) thought it a very con- siderable sum to be got in two months. He thought it reflected the appreciation of the work of the Associa- tion. (Hear' hear.) He then moved a resolution thanking the Mayor for raising the money. Councillor FULTON-SMITH seconded. He said the Mayor's effort had been more than successful and it had succeeded in removing a great cloud over the work of the Association. With the same footing which the Association was now on, he thought that the nurses and everybody else who were connected with the Association would be a great deal easier in mind and could therefore do their work better. It was one of the best institutions and he thought no association at ' the present time accomplished such results as the Nursing Association. (Hear, hear.) The MAYOR said he was very much obliged for the way the resolution had been carried. He felt that it , was time something was done to help such an Associa- tion as the donors had helped. When he entered the Council some eight or ten years ago he thought that as 'thil people of the town had done so much for him he would try and do something for them. After they had put him in the Council Chamber he was appointed a magistrate, and then the town made him an alderman. Aft-r that they made him Mayor of the town, an office which he never thought he would be able to till. When he went to a meeting of the Nursing Association he was informed that it was in debt, and he offered, without thinking what the result would be, to raise the amount. He had great pleasure in handing to the Treasurer a cheque for £356 4s. 6d. (Applause.) Father WILSON proposed a vote of thanks to the donors, and said that they bad responded to the Mayor's appeal in a manner which showed their appreciation of the work of the Association, The money would enable the nurses to ensure a wider interest in their work. Councillor BARTON seconded and expressed the hope that the Mayor's example would be followed by future Mayors. (F-Tear, hear.) Mr. C. E. PARKER responded on behalf of the donors and suggested that they should buy the Mayor at his own valuation and sell him at any valuation that the town liked. (Applause.) He (Mr. Parker) wiuld be able to make some money out of that. In order that the Association could be placed on even a sounder footing he also suggested that every subscriber should double his subscription. (Hear, hear.) Mr. J. D. FAIRCLOUGH proposed a vote of thanks to the Chairman. Mr. H. HOPE seconded and the metiou was carried.

The iiO;:.i..VC;;-G.E. in reply said that was an occasion when he felt proud to live in Warrington. They got the people to respond so readily to the extension of the Infirmary and now they had got them to subscribe liberally to the Nursing Association, which was very gratifying. He suggested that the Association should have a house to house collection and then the popula- tion generally wouldle able to show their appreciation of the work done by that Association. (Applause.) The meeting then terminated.

div.head: REACHED TOO FAR.
div.p: REACHED TOO FAR.

At Widnes, on Monday, John Connolly, Edward Goulding, Albert Goulding, and John Lyon were charged with stealing from John Corcoran 9s. 2}(l. The prisoners adopted a rather ingenious method. They were drinking in the bar of the Britannia Vaults, when the unwary youth quickly fell a victim to their plans. After a little conversation the prisoners discussed who could reach the farthest up the side of the wall. Corcoran was invited to try, and he readily agreed. As soon as he stretched out his arm his hands were pinned and his pockets ransacked. Information was given to the police, and the four were arrested. Connolly, when charged said, "You cannot arrest four of us for robbery. The others know nothing about it."—Albert Goulding, whose record was not so bad as the others, was sent to gaol for two months ; the other three were each sent to prison for three months.

It is obvious that a, large THE PRESS number of Press represen- AND THE tatives would be an

FRONTIER WAR. encumbrance of a rather serious character to such a small force as that which is operating in exceed- ingly awkward coantry against the Zakka Kb°ls. No general in command would like to be respon- sible to any extent whatever for the safety of newspaper correspondents accompanying an army under such conditions. Yet we cannot profess to be satisfied with the answer given by Mr. MORLEY in the House of Commons on this subject. It was an answer which, ' after the Scotch manner, asked another ques- tion. "Does my hon. friend," said the INDIAN SECRETARY, referring to Mr. SWIFT MACNEILL, "mean that I should exercise a Press censorship in India? " Mr. SWIFT MecNarLes retort was admirably to the point. "What I mean," he said, "is whether Lord KITCHENER is to exercise the Press censorship." This question covers a very large subject for consideration. Soldiers in positions of command do not in these days like to be accompanied by men who will in any case, be a I burden, and may be possible critics of their opera- tions. They would themselves, of course,put their case on higher grounds. They would say that the facilities for communication have been so extended of late years that a newspaper correspondent may, without any evil intentions whatever, place the enemy in possession or the plan of operations against him. In this case, however, such an argument does not apply. Newspaper correspon- dents are actually accompanying the force which is operating against the Zikk% Khels. "The Times " and " The Daily Mail" are represented,as Mr. MORLEY admitted. Permission to be repro. sented appears to have been refused to an Indian News Agency. The refusal is intelligible on the ground just stated. Information published in Indian newspapers might make its way to the hills before the operations were ooncluded.
But, granting that there might be danger in telegrams sent from the scene of this small war and immediately published in Calcutta, Lahore, or Bombay, wa must insist that we cannot see any
los

reason whatever why two English papers-should be favoured after the announcement had been made that no correspondents were toaccompany the expedition. If there was to be any relaxation of this rule, it should certainly have been in favour of the English Press generally, through the news agencies, and not merely in favour of the two newspapers, to which the :permission to send representatives to the hill country is not only a considerable commercial advantage, but is also a measure calculated to keep the bulk of the readers of newspapers at home from the most immediate supply of news as to what is being done by the force under General WILLMES. We may at once add that this is not likely to happen. The English Press has more means of getting informa- tion than can be controlled by generals in the field or by War Office at home. The movement against the presence of news- paper representatives in campaigns was started by Lord WOLsELEIC many years ago, when he pub- lished his " Soldier's Pocket Book." Yet Lord WoLsELBY, though he established in Egypt a censorship over Press telegrams, has never restricted, or has only restricted to the smallest extent, the number of newspaper correspondents accompanying any operations which he bas corn- mended. Lord KITCHENNit has, in this respect, been much more severe. Then censorship in South Africa was strict beyond reason. Japan, taking the hiot from him, virtually converted the European special correspondents into prisoners. The question that demands an answer which it does not at present seem likely to get, is whether it would be to the national advantage to suppress • the war correspondent altogether, including, of course, the officer on active service who sends • information to newspapers. Should wars, that is to say, be conducted in secret ? Did reply to ' such an inquiry must necessarily have reference to the fact that it was a newspaper correspondent who saved our army in the Crimea.

In another column Messrs. MIMES. FAIRCLOUGH James Fairclough and Sons, AND THE BECIDGB. Ltd., ask for" a little space to meet some of the remarks recently made about ria." After a care- ful perusal of the firm's letter we cannot find that they have touched even the fringe of recent criticism of their attitude on this much vexed question. At the last Conncil meeting, the Mayor stated that the provision of a new bridge at a cost to the town of £lB,OOO or £20,000 would enable Messrs. Fairclough to effect a saving in water carriage of a sum which he computed at £7BO a year. Towards the cost of a new bridge the firm had offered £l,OOO, which the Council considered inadequate when compared with the advantage to Messrs. Fairclough. We should have thought that this criticism by the Mayor of the Borouge would have been worthy the attention of Messrs. Fair- dough, but in replying specially " to the remarks recently made" they make no allusion whatever to the Mayor's statement. This is surely a serious omission from a document which professes to be argukientative. In fact Messrs. Fairclough's letter is siffgularly lacking in cogent reasons why the scheme for widening the present bridge by canti- levers should not be proceeded with. They certainly make it very clear that the present bridge is awk- ward to navigate and that they fervently desire a new one, but we think they quite fail to prove that the widening scheme would add seriously to the difficulties of navigation. Even with a new bridge.' which would probably be wider than the present structure with its cantilever footpaths, the fiatinan would still have to lower his funnel and put the , helmsman in a " smother " of smoke. It seems to us that a little careful stoking would provide an easy way out of this difficulty—and we offer the suggestion for what it is w u•tti. From the point of view of the people of 'Warrington, the widening of the, present bridge would meet all requirements for several years at a reasonable cost, and we see no reason to alter our opinion that the scheme could be carried out without adding to the handicap which Nature end the bridge builders al bygone years have placed upon Messrs. Fairclough's water carriage. If a new bridge were absolutely essential we should be glad to think that they, as Warring- ton traders, would benefit thereby, but we do not think that the town is called upon to incur need- less expense to suit Messrs. Fairclough's conveni- ence.

"If we are going to found Ts/draftslion the prosperity of the country, Itsronar. its commercial prosperity, its industrial prosperity, upon an impregnable basis, we must cleanse the foundation from the rot of alcohol." These are the words of Mr. D. Lloyd George M.P., uttered at the annual meeting of the United Kingdom Alliance in October! last. They emphasise the need for temperance reform, which was never more imperative than now. The Act of 1904 gave the brewers a vested interest in the licences, which they have endeavoured to sabstantiate by all manner of specious argument and special pleading. Magisterial control over the licences has been weakened, and popular control never appeared more remote. But the Government of to-day has a mandate from the country to deal drastically with the trade which has been so bolstered up in the past by privilege and class legislation. There must be a short time limit to the compensation clauses of 1904 which created the vested interest in a licence, and the principle of self•government and popular control must be definitely established. As the Premier has said "this is the foundation of our eduza - Copal policy ; it is the foundation of our licensing policy." A meeting under the auspices of the United Kingdom Alliance was held in Parr Hall on Wednesday evening, and if the size of the audience was hardly commensurate with the importance of the occasion there was no mistaking the enthu- siasm of the representative reformers who assembled. Resolutions were passed on lines indicated by the policy foreshadowed above in order to strengthen the hands of the G wernment in framing the Bill which is promised for an early date. Canon Hicks and Mr. Sloan, M.P. were the principal speakers, and the persuasive eloqu- ence of the former was admirably adapted to voicing the demands of the temperance reformer in 'a reasonable and convincing manner. Mr. Sloan evidenced the national Irish characteristics of humour and direct- ness, and in style the two speeches were admirably contrasted. LDC%I option is the irreducible minimum of the Alliance, and both speakers argued logically and effectively for popular control. Mr. DAds and the Rev. J. F. Matthews touched upon tempeeance topics which had a local application, and the former announced amid cheers that he was willing to put his hand to the plough and develop the work commenced that night if the friends of temperance in Warrington were in earnest. It is high time we had an awakening of reforming zeal in Warrington, and we hope soon to sea in actual operation some such effective municipal body as a Temperance Electoral Council, which was advocated and supported in this paper a few months ago. The work has commenced. We trust it will continue until the people of Warring- ton—and of the whole country —have the will and the power to say where and when they will or will not have licences in their midst.

As was anticipated, the TIIII EDUCATIONAL estimates of the Education BURMIN. Committee involving an advance in the rate of 2id. were passed en Monday without a dissentient voice. After Mr. Jolley's clear statement of the cause of the increased demand there was no course to adopt but to sanction it and look as pleasant as possible under the circumstances. Ode of the most important matters which will con- front the committee during the coming year is

the medical inspection of school children for ' which £5OO has been set aside. Already the committee has taken steps to put the Act into operation, and two appointments have been sanctioned. The matter was discussed at some length on Monday evening, but that was before the reporters were admitted, and at the public meeting it was allowed to pass without comment. A lady is vo be appointed as assistant medical adviser of the Education Committee to perform, under the supervision of the medical adviser, the duty of inspection of schools and other duties consequent thereon, and her salary will be £225 per annum. In addition there is to be a school nurse, with a salary of £BO and uniform, to act as home visitor. She will, as far as possible, deal with all cases of absence from school through sickness, except those on account of infectious disease which come within the province of the Public Health Thpartment. Owing to the want of accommodation in some of the schools, it will be necessary to form centres for the purpose of con- ducting the examination of children, and probably six centres (preferably schools) will be sufficient. The decisions of the Committee appear to be on sound lines, and we believe a great gain to the community may be anticipated from a careful administration of the Act. It is particularly satisfactory to note that the homes where sickness prevails will be visited by a trained nurse, for in sadly too many cases children are hampered in the MCO of life through parental igoorance. If the outcome of the visits is that parents will be better instructed in the methods of combating the ailments to which the children are subject, the innovation will meet with the approval of all right- thinking townspeople.

div.head: NOTES AND NOTIONS.
div.p: NOTES AND NOTIONS.

The Mayor deserves the thanks of the people of Warrington for having raised in two months the sum of .£356 to relieve from debt that valuable public institution, the Nursing Association. His whip-up was very cordially responded to, and we should think he is fully entitled to claim the Begging Championship of Warrington. * * *

Mr. J. A. Meddon, the-Member for the Newton Division, had letter be on his guard and get his election machinery in order. Mr. J. H. Bottomly, the Conservative agent for that district, speaking at Padgate said " he expected the General Election.to be next March." One wonders whether he is in touch with Sir Henry Campbell-Bannerman. In any case no doubt the wish is father to the expectation. * * * Next week we shall commence a series of special articles on Free Trade versus Pretection by Mr. L. G. Chiozza Money, ALP., who is widely recognised as one of the first authorities on social problems, and particularly the fiscal question. Mr. Money's articles are written in a homely and uuderstandable style which should make them specially attractive, and his arguments are put so conclusively that Tariff Reform is made to look exactly what it is—a hollow pretence. Begin to read the series next week with Mr. Money's first article " Ought we to fear imports ? " and we are sure you will follow them week by week with keen appreciation.

The mysterions disappearance of the Dublin State jewels has had one curious parallel which seems to have escaped notice. Some years ago a casket con- taining jewels of the value of £13,000 disappeared, under circumstances of the greatest mystery, from the house of the Duchess of Leinster in Dominic-street, Dublin. In spite of the most thorough investigation no trace of the thieves could be discovered, although rumour suggested that more than one person of rank could throw light on the robbery. The jewels were ultimately returned to their noble owner ; but to this day, we believe, the mystery of their disappearance remains unsolved. _ * 5 *.

Tory electioneerers are ;gain in luck—our butter is casting us more, sometimes as much as threepence per pound. If this had only been worked at South Leeds, perhaps even that fortress might have fallen. Someone suggested that the rise was due to a corner in produce, but the " Times " assures us that there is nothing in the suggestion. "It is a bona fide scarcity due to absence of rain in Ausiralia and New Zealand." Exactly—even the heavens are brass in their anger at the slamming of the door on the Colonial Prefer- ence. Our mouth waters (says the " Westminster Gazette ") for the Big Pat which would have been our happy lot had there only been in office a Government which, by deciding to accept the Colonial" oiler," had brought the rain down in Australia.

* * Our good friend Alderman Bennett is usually con- sidered an authority on local affairs, but when expounding Imperial policy he occasionally gets out of his latitude. He is, like a few others, very keen on Tariff Reform. Speaking at the Conservative meeting at Padgate last Tuesday, he stated that "one of the most foolish things the Government had done was to take off the Coal ,Tax." Now if Alderman Bennett resided in a colliery district, he would have come to exactly the contrary opinion, for Colliery Proprietors Miners and Ship Owners, who ought to know, all con- demned the tax, arid sent deputations to the Govern- ment praying for its removal. As a matter of fact,the tax led not only to the ranks of the unemployed being increased, both colliers and sailors being thrown out lof work, but wages were also reduced 10 per cent. We commend the study of the Coal and Sugar taxes 11 and how they affected employment and wages, to the study not,only of Alderman Bennett, but also of other would-be Tariff Reformers.

* * * Saturday, being the second anniversary of Stockton Heath Tree Planting Day, presented a favourable opportunity to the Heathens to give full vent to their indignation at the recent wanton damage done to many of the trees in the village. Needless to say, they rose to the occasion and the dictionaries must have been carefully scanned to find strong enough words to apply to the miscreant. The following are a few of the beautiful expressions to which utterance was given in describing the perpetrator of this outrage which has staggered Stockton Heath : Hooligan,. Impudent desperado. Pest of Society. Murderer. Insidious Viper. Incendiary and midnight assassin. One in league with darkness and the devil. It is perhaps needless to add that most of the picture- sque epithets formed part of the speech of Dr. Parker who has earned renown as the orator of the move- ment. * * *

There were some sad rjelations at an inquest in Warrington on Monday, relative to the death of the six-weeks old child of Arthur and Mary Glover, 3 Buckley-street. In January, 1907, an inquest was held on a previous child of the same parents. The verdict in each case was one of "natural causes," but the woman was given the character of an habitual drunkard who neglected her home and was linable to withstand temptation. Coroner Brighouse seemed • rather sorry for the woman at first and suggested that " some of her predecessors were responsible for her present weakness of character." Then his mood changed, and he told the husband -a respectable, hard-workingman—to " give her a good hanamering and never mind if the magistrates convict you for assault." It is interesting to know that this is the course Mr. Brighouse would take with an erring wife, but the offering of such advice by an officer of the Crown in open court is to be deplored. If Glover took the Coroner's advice too readily and literally, Mr. Brighouse might find himself in the unhappy position of inquiring into the cause of a tragedy from which be w as directly responsible. _

The Labour party seemed determined to go on with their project of running a Labour daily newspaper. A. special Conference to consider ways and means will be held in London on Wednesday° under the auspices of the Trade Union Congress, Parliamentary Com- mittee. The proposals include the formation of a limited company with a capital of .£lOO,OOO in il shares. The projected paper is to be a halfpenny eight-page daily with a title of " The 'Morning Herald." With the sad fate of the "Tribune" before them, the Labour men had best hasten slowly. £1.00,003 does , not go far in the establishment of an up-to-date " daily," and the market shows signs of being over- loaded. The rate of mortality among metropolitan newspapers is decide Ily high. During the last twelve years the folio sing daily papers have co tsed public t- tion in London :-" Daily Courier," "Daily Paper," " Morning Herald," " Sun," " Ech " tjority," "Tribune." Of these, toe " Iltjmity," with its five issues, was the mos; short-lival, aid " P.:31).3" (18138-1905) the most long-live-I. Two other dailies - the Iforning and the St. James's Gazette -have within the same interval been merged in other publications.

Liberal Ward Meetings. During the past week a number of ward meetings for the election of officers &c.. have been held and have been largely attended. The annual meeting of he Liberal Association is to be held next week. 'LINSEED COMPOUND' for Coughs and Colds Relieves Asthma and difficult breathing.—Advt.

Elective Auditors. The election of two elective auditors will take place on March 2nd. The present holders of the offices are Messrs L. Bolton and E. England. So far the candi- dates nominated are Messrs. E. England and \V. Chrimes.

A Rough Customer. At the Warrington Police C ,art, on Thursday morning, Mary M'llonald, of no settled abode, was sent to gaol for one month on charges of obscene language, wilful damage, and assault. On Wednesday she visited a lodging-house in Rose and Crown-street and broke two panes of glass. When Jenks, the lodging-house-keeper,went to her she struck him twice in the face and need obscene language.

LINSEED COMPOUND,' Trade— Mark of Kays Compound Essence of Linseed for Coughs S.: Colds.--Ad vt Warrington and District Baptist Union. The winter meetings in connection with the above Union were held at the Baptist Church, Golborne- street, on Thursday when delegates, members, and friends attached to the Warringtont Latchford, Hill Cliffe, and Little Leigh Baptise churches attended. At the business meeting in th; afternoon it was decided to hold the next meeting of the Association at Latchford in May next. In the afternoon a service was conducted in the chapel by Professor Ellis, M.A., of Manchester Baptist College, who took his text from Joshua iii. 5, 'Sanctify yourselves, for to-morrow the Lord will do wondrous things for you." After the service a tea was served in the schoolroom over which Mrs. Few, Mrs. Wynne Jones, Mrs. Pepper and Mrs. Fernley presided. In the evening a public meeting was held in the chapel pre- ided over by the Vice-President, the Rev. A. Hum, of Little Leigh, in the absence through indisposition of the President, Mr. R. Billington. The speakers were Professor Ellis and the Rev. A. Hardy of Widnes, who gave very instructive and inspiring addresses. Although the meetings were not so largely attended as usual, the tone of the addresses reached a high standard.
