div.head: CHILDREN'S SUMMER CARP. -- Annual Meeting of the Committee.
div.p: CHILDREN'S SUMMER CARP. -- Annual Meeting of the Committee.
The annual meeting of the Committee of the War- rington Children's Summer Camp was held at the Old Academy on Thursday evening, the Rev. W. Bracecamp in the chair. There was a large attendance.
TREASURER'S REPORT.

The TREASURER (Mr. Ransome) read his report in which he said that as shown on the balance sheet the account was still considerably overdrawn at the bank. The number of children sent to the camp was not quite as many as last year, but the committee felt that until they were on a sounder financial basis it was unwise to send more children than can be paid for by the money received during the year. They would thus see that it was of the utmost importance that money should be sent in early,at any rate before the end of June,in order that the committee can decide how many they can afford to send. The balance sheet was adopted.

div.head: SECRETARY'S HEPORT.
div.p: SECRETARY'S HEPORT.

Mr. W. H. J. JENECItti presented his annual report as follows :—" The adverse balance of 4.231 la. 3d. incurred, mainly for establishment expenses, was not a cheering factor with which to begin the se tson's work. Mr. A. H. Lee having resigned the office of hon. treasurer the Committee are to be congratulated OR Mr. John A. Ransome accepting the position. By the exer- cise of prudence and economy the debit balance has been reduced to £139 13s. 4d. The responsibilities of the Committee were much relieved by the following gentlemen guaranteeing the overdraft to the Bank : Messrs. Joseph Beswick, W. H. J. Jenkins. J. A. Ransome, J. W. Slack, F. G. Taylor, Louis Henshall. William Owen, and J. H. Smethurst. The number of children taken to camp Was 202 boys and IES girls. Although the weather during the season was somewhat broken, the children thoroughly enjoyed the holiday in camp. It was attended by highly beneficial results to their health. A much larger number of adult visitors from Warrington than hitherto took advantage of the inducements to visit and spend their holidays in the camp. Without exception, pleasure and satisfaction at the accommodation provided was expressed by the visitors. This development has materially helped the funds. The new caretaker and his wife, Mr. and Mrs. Whitney, did their work in a painstaking and satisfactory manner. The warmest thanks of the sub- scribers are due to the voluntary superintendents and their staffs :—Girls' superintendent : Mrs. Wilkinson. Assistant officers : Misses Emson, Downes. Birch, Larson, and Sumner. Boys' superintendents : (first week) Mr. A. H. Lee. (Second week) Mr. Thorold D. , Lee. Assistant offioers : Messrs. Christopher Lee, Griffiths, Houghton' Jolley, Mee, Newton, W. Turner, and W. H. Turner. The Director of Education (Mr. J. Moore Murray) and his staff have again rendered great assistance in the selection of the children, and Mr. Charles White has also examiaed and passed the children prior to going to camp, and their services are greatly appreciated. The thanks a the committee are also due to those who have made special efforts on behalf of the funds, viz. : Warrington Catholic Amateur Dramatic Society, proceeds of the performances of "The Ticket-of-leave Man," £2O ; Peoples College, annual collection and hooks, £l4 Os. lid. ; Officers Ist,. V.B. South Lancashire Regiment, £5 55. ; St. Paul's Church, collection at volunteer parade service, £4 4s. ; Heathside Schools, normal collection and books, £2 Ms. Bd. ; Warrington Training College, annual collection, £9. 10s. ; Wycliffe Congregational Church, collection, £2 Bs. Bd. ; Mr. A. H. Lee, for bath fund, £1 ISi. 2d. ; Fairfield Schools' Bazaar, part proceeds, El. Enquiries are being made as to the advisability of opening the Camp earlier than in previous seasons, and this is a matter which will receive the careful attention of the Committee. It is pleasing to record the fact that the Mayor and Mayoress, and a , number of friends visited the Clow daring the past season. There is little doubt that the kindly interest taken by the visitors, who expressed every satisfaction lat the facilities afforded for the welfare of the children and visitors, will give an impetus to the work of the Committee. Mr. E. J. HALL in moving the adoption of the secretary's report congratulated Mr. Jenkins on the way he had done the work. Mr. P. O. TAYLOR seconded and the report was I adopted. ELECTION OF OFFICERS.

The CHAITIMADT proposed that Lady Greenall be elected president of the Association. Mr. LONGLAND seconded and the motion was carried unanimously. The committee was selected as follows :—Mesdames Dakin, Forshaw, floury Roberts, Wilkinson, James, Richardson, Ewart, Gibson, Ransome, and Loneland ; and Messra.L. Ifenshall,A. ELLee,Moore Murray, Parker, J. H. Smethurst, T. Ashcroft, Cox, Bracecalup and Taylor. Mr. Hansome was re-elected treasurer and Mr, Jenkins secretary. Votes of thanks concluded the meeting.

div.head: PALACE AND HIPPODROME.
div.p: PALACE AND HIPPODROME.

One of the best variety entertainments ever seen in Warrington is presented at the Palace and Hippodrome this week, and has afforded delight to large audiences. The great attraction is provided by Lew Lake and his comedy company, who appear in a farcical absurdity "The Bloomsbury Burglars " and its sequel, a petite comedy drama "My Pal Jerry." Both sketches are excellent, the adventures of the droll cracksmen keeping the house in a state of merriment. The trial scene is ludicrous in the extreme, the judge and officers of the Court being terrorised by the prisoners who while away the time by furious onslaughts on all and sundry and cool attempts to escape. There is a touch of pathos in the last scene, one of the "pals " being shot whilst escaping from prison and expiring just as th 3 warders overtake the fugitives. The parting of the convicts is most affecting. As Jerry Jackson and Nobbler Nolan respectively, Bob Morris and Lew Lake are the life and soul of the per- formance and are rewarded with rounds of applause. The Bros. Ashley score a great success in their smart boxing comedy sketch "Next please" which winds up with a laughable boxing act. Kit Keen is a clever coloured comedian and his selections on the " bones " prove most popular. Rosie Revel, comedy Dutch boy and burlesque coon, gives one of the most pleasing turns of the evening and Gertie Moore does admirably in her singing and dancing speciality. Unfortunately the Rohda Bros., who present an exceptionally fine gymnastic act, were only able to appear on Monday evening, one of them having been laid up with influenza for the rest of the week. The animated pictures are, as usual, up to date and interesting, while Widdop and his orchestra provide capital music.

div.head: LOCAL PARLIAMENT.
div.p: LOCAL PARLIAMENT.
LICENSING BILL PASSED.
The Cld-Age Pensions Bill.

The first measure foreshadowed in the King's Speech —the Licensing Bill—has now been passed through our local House of Commons, and the Government are to be congratulated on their triumph in the division which was taken on Thursday evening. There was a consider- ably larger attendance of members and public than at last week's sitting and the debate on the whole was more interesting.

div.head: QUESTION TIME.
div.p: QUESTION TIME.
The questions of which notice had been given were more numerous than usual. _

In replying to the Member for East Mayo (who was not present) the Prime Minister said the Government proposed to take the question of Ireland into considera- tion in the order in which it stood in the King's Speech. t The Meraber for Carlow inquired whether it was the intention of the Government to extend the compulsory powers of the Land Purchase Act of 1903 to Ireland? Mr. J. F. AWBERY (secretary for Ireland) said it was not the intention of the Government to add any measures to those already foreshadowed in the King's Speech, but they sincerely hoped that an opportunity might present itself later, if they continued in office, to deal not only with the land question but with self- government for Ireland in such a manner as would 'close the unfortunate chapters in Irish history (Ministerial cheers). i Mr. G. H. W. STEEL (Northwich) asked if the ; Government would consider the question of imposing a tax of Is. in the .£ on all betting transactions and racing stakes and granting licences subject to strict supervision to bookmakers and turf commissioners, representing a yield of 2i millions ? The PREMIER: No, sir. This Government would never attempt to raise money by legalising vice. (Ministerial cheers). Mr. H. HAYES (Somerset West) asked if the Govern- ment would consider the suggestion of imposing a tax on titles, representing a yield of two millions ? The PREMIER said that in every civilized community there must be rewards offered to those who had deserved well of the State. There might be two opinions as to what those deserts were, but having given honours it would be a graceless act to tax the recipients. I The Rev. J. F. MlTTilsws (Merthyr Tydvil) asked ' whether in view of the trouble arising oat of the raid of suffragists on the House of Commons the Premier would introduce legislation dealing with the whole -question of women's suffrage. The PRISSIER : This Government will never intro- 'duce legislation for the sake of avoiding trouble—. (laughter)—but I may say the childish and law-breaking methods adopted by the advocates of women's suffrage ;at the present day make the Government hesitate to I artvance along the line suggested by the hon. member's question.

THE LICENSING BILL. I Amendments by the Opposition proposing the refund- ing of contribntions to the compensation fund to those whose licences were not renewed ; that new licences shonid be put up for sale by auction and the proceeds applied to the extinction of liceoces in congested areas were defeated. On an amendment by Mr. EYRES (Worcester), pro- hibiting canvassing by the promotor or an objector to a proposed new licence being submitted, The PREMIER said that if his friend would introduce a Bill to prohibit canvassing in any ciroumstances whatever, he would receive hearty support from that side of the House. So long as canvassing was allowed ' ;in every other direction the Government could not I accept the amendment. I On the amendment being put to the vote, it was I carried by 76 to 35. Mr. W. L. WILLIAMS (Oswestry) introduced an amendment to the clause prohibiting children under 14 years of age to be in the public or business portion of lan on-licensed house. He proposed to add the words : ' Unless accompanied by its parent or guardian or the iwife or husband of such parent or guardian." He con- tended that the clause as it stood was grandmotherly I legislation and implied distrust of licence holders. It was also an injustice to the parents. ' Mr. S. W. JEFFERY (High Peak Division, Minister for Eduoation) said the amendment would entirely ( destroy the clause. Surely it must be lamentable for ; anyone to pass through Warrington streets and see I parents going into public-houses with young children. Why should a child be brought into an atmosphere such as that without any of its own will being called into play? Mr. E. PLINST3N (Gateshead), in supporting the clause said that as a representative of trade unionism he believed workingmen were doing themselves, their children and their cause a wrong by meeting for busi- ness purposes within a public-house. On a vote being taken the amendment was defeated by 67 votes to 46. Mr. W. H. STANSFIELD (Dublin University) had given notice of amendment that where total Sunday closing is observed it should apply to clubs as well as to licensed premises. The PRIME AMSTER : We accept that amendment. (Cheers). Mr. GORDON PITT (South Leeds) speaking on the Bill as a whole said it would not go one-tenth of the distance he personally would like to go. The Bill he would enforce 'would be the complete abolition or on-licences. He, however, supported the Bill as it tended to a reduction of licences. Councillor NIELD said the Government had shown more anxiety about the rights of majorities than for temperance reform. Se long as they had a majority, the people could go for salvation if they liked or they could go to the---(here the Member made an expres- sive pause.) Councillor Nield caused the greatest laugh of the evening when referring to systems in force in foreign lands. He seemed uncertain as to the name of the scheme in force in Norway, but after a pause ventured the statement that it was on Swedenborgian lines. When the mirth had subsided he said : I mean the Gothenburg system. (Laughter). The Rev. J. F. MATTIIEWS : lam pleased the hon. member is interested in theology. (Laughter). The•Puumthrt said the Bill was not primarily a tem- perance measure, but a democratic measure. He was bound to confess that a scheme of local option if adopted in this country would probably tell against the temperance people. It would in some cases lead to an increase in licences and he was prepared to accept tha t as a democrat. He was prepared to put the power in the hands of the people to regulate and control the traffic. The Bill was fair and just to the licence holder. It gave him full and fair warning of what might happen seven years hence. The Government had taken care to protect those who could not protect themselves— helpless little children. On the amendment that the Bill be read that day six months being put, 52 votes were recorded for it and 82 I against. It is interesting to note that no Socialists i voted for the amendment, only four Nationalists, and ' one Independent. The Bill as am ended was then passed. OLD AGE PENSIONS BILL.

A Bill for the provision of old age pensions was laid on the table and will be introduced next week by Mr. J. Morton (President of the Local Government Board). Its provisions are : (1,) On and after June Ist, 1008 every British sub- ject who has resided within the United Kingdom for 40 years and who has attained the age of 65 years shall be entitled to receive by a fund created and maintained by monies provided by Parliament and °ailed the State I Pension Fund, a sum of ss. per week for life. (2) The State Pension Fund shall be established and meintained by annual grants made by Parliament. (3) The State Pension Fund shall be administered as a department of the Post Olice under the direction of the Post Master General who shall issue from time to time such instructions as he may deem necessary for carrying out the intention of this Act, but such instructions must conform to the following require- ments. •

(1) Application for and payment of pension shall be made at the Post Office most convenient to the pensioner. (2) After proof of age by applicant and identification by the Post Office staff, a certificate shall be issued to the pensioner,which certificate may be required to be produced at each payment. (3) Pensions may be paid weekly, monthly, or quarterly as may snit the pensioner, but 114 in advance.

(4) Every assignment and charge upon a State pension, and every agreement to assign or charge a State pension shall except so far as made for the benefit of the family of thei pensioner IDD void, and on the bankruptcy of a pensioner, pensions shall not pass to any trustee or other person acting on behalf of the creditors. _ _
The Society will meet nest week on Wednesday at 7.30.

Paper Mills to be Erected.

We understand, that land has been purchased on the banks of the river in the Howley district, Warrington, on which it is proposed to erect mills for manufacturing paper, for Messrs. Joseph Chadwick and Sons, of Oldham, who are removing from there to Warrington, in consequence of the difficulties in obtaining female and other labour,caused by the great demands in the Cotton Trade. We understand that the new works will give employment to several hundreds of hands The tenders for the ereetiou of the works have already been sent , in.

Under the auspices of the Lancashire and Cheshire Conservative Workine Men's Federation there was a , special Convention on Saturday at the Earlestown ' Town Hall, under the presidency of Sir Henry Seton- IKarr. In the circular calling the meeting it was stated the Council of the Federation had arranged to hold this , " demonstration of trade unionists and others to protest against the compulsory ' payment towards the Partia- -1 mentar3; funds of such unions,whichconstitutes an injus- tice to a large number of Conservative, and also Liberal working men, who are thereby compelled to contribute through their unions to the upkeep and Parliamentary • expenses of Socialistic and other doctrinaires holding political views utterly at variance with the recognised order of society." It was announced from the chair in i the course of the meeting that delegates were present from eighty towns of Lancashire and Cheshire and from , a hundred branches of the Federation. I Sir Henry Seton-Karr, in opening the meeting, said 1 there were at least two solid grounds why the members ! of trade unions had good reason to object to this com- pulsory contribution. Trade unions were not political , organisations. (Hear, hear.) They were legalised in order that the members might hold their own in the ; case of disputes between capital and labour,and another object was that the funds should be used for sick and ;burial purposes and, in case of disputes, for strike pay. I These were not political or party objects. It was lobvious tie-it these funds, which were subscribed for non-party purposes' were not to be used for party purposes. (Hear, hear.) There was another serious , objection. LABOUR MEMBERS OF PARLIAMENT. What kind of Parliamentary represent Rives had they ,to support? He had the privilege of being a member I of the House of COmmons for something like twenty years, and in his time he was acqueinted with some I Labour representatives who were high-principled, worthy-minded men. But there was one broad charac- teristic. They were nearly all Radicals or Liberals. Scarcely one voted with the Conservative party. The position had changed a good deal, and the number of I Labour members had increased to about fifty. At the last election a great Labour wave went through the , constituencies, and men returned members of their own 1 class to represent them. What had happened since then ? They had read of the extraordinary proceedings at the Hull Conference,and for himself he was uncertain where Labour ended and Where Socialism began. He could not help thinking that the Socialist tail was beginning to wag the Labour dog. (Hear, hear.) To his mind the policy they were pursuing was one of the most dangerous policies ever advocated in this country, and the pity of it was that it was a policy calculated not only injure injure the country as a whole, but in parti- cular to the very men they professed to represent —the wage-earning class of this country. (Applause.) PROTEST AGAINST SUPPORTING SOCIALISTS. Sir. George Gregsoa (Bury) proposed the following resolution. "That in the opinion of this meeting of trade unionists and others, the compulsory contributions to Parliamentary funds for the upkeep of Socialistic representatives in Parliament is a grave injustice to the political convictions of a large body of both Conservative and Liberal trade unionists, and this meeting urges upon members of Parliament the desirabillity of an amendment of the law which shall make these contributions optional instead of compulsory." Mr. T. Shivers (Blackburn), a representative of weavers, seconded the resolution, and spoke strongly against the persistent efforts of Socialists to make con- verts at the factory gate and in conversation with workers to show them they ought to have more Labour representatives. Mr. William Webster (Bryn), who was announced as a • Liberal, and who said it was his first appearance on a Conservative platform, and that he came forward also as a Roman Catholic, supported the resolution. The resolution *as further supported by Messrs. J. Fellows (Bury), A. Radcliffe (Hay), T. Atkinson (Liverpool), and T. Dickinson (St. Helens), and carried unanimously. Mr. W. Joynson-Hicks afterwards addressed the meet- ing, and, as on his arrival, was received with great enthusiasm. div.p: ST. HELENS.
RUNCORN AND WIDNES
FRAUDS AT ST. HELENS.

On Saturday at the St. Helens Police Court, James Beard, who has several aliases and who is at present , undergoing a term of eighteen months' imprisonment at Preston gaol, was charged with fraud and theft. The , evidence showed that the prisoner, representing that he was a member of a wholesale firm of fruiterers com- mencing business in the town, obtained lodgings in ' three different houses in succession, then left without paying, and also stole various things, including a gold watch and albert, value £ll. Beard was arrested at Preston for a theft there, and wrote to a Wigan publican enclosing the pawaticksts for the watch and chain, and asking him to sell the tickets, as he wanted money for his defence. The publican sent him 425. He was sentenced to a further eleven months' imprisonment, to follow his Preston sentence.

div.head: LABOUR PARTY'S PROGRAMAE.
div.p: LABOUR PARTY'S PROGRAMAE.

MR. T. GLOVER, 1.P., AT ST. HELENS. Speaking at a meeting at St. Helens on Saturday night in connection with the Amalgamated Union of Labourers, Mr. T. Glover, M.P., said that since the Hull Conference it had been stated that there was a split in the Labour party and that the party had been taken over by the Socialists. He could tell them that there was no dissension iu the ranks of the party in Parliament. They had held their meetings, and decided what bills to bring before the House if they got the chance. The first bill was the Unemployed Workmen's • Bill, then the Sweated Industries and Minimum Wage Bill, the Provision of Meals for Children in Scotland, , Compulsory Weights and Measures Bill, the Exporta- tion and Importation of" Blacklegs," and the General Eight Hours question. They would agree with him that those were bills, if they could only get them passed, which would be a benefit to the workers of this ' country. The great question of old-age pensions had not been mentioned, because it was in the King's Speech, and so they could not put any name down in the ballot for it. He was pleased to be able to inform them that the Government did intend to pass an old-age pension bill this session, and that ihe Chancellor of the Exchequer had decided to put aside eight millions during the session, which, with the two and a half millions which he had ear-marked before, would make ten and a half millions to commence old-age pensions. If they could get in this end of the wedge he thought it would be a good thing for the workers and the old warriors of the country that they would be able, instead of having to seek the workhouse as a refuge, to live comformbly by hemaelves or ytto their friaa Is. (Applause.)

div.head: LABOUR PARTY AND SOCIALIST
div.p: LABOUR PARTY AND SOCIALIST

We have been told by the capitalist Press that the delegates at the annual Conference acted inconsistently by rejecting Socialism one day, and then accepting a Socialist resolution the following. As one of those who voted with the majority on each occasion I don't admit any inconsistency. What are the facts? An amendment to alter the constitution was sub- mitted by the Paper Stainers' Union. If the amend- ment had been carried it would have been to impose Socialism as a condition of membership. In my opinion it would have been a serious mistake —as well as unfair to the trades unions --to impose a condition which would exclude a vary large majority of the present members. The compact on which the Labour party is based is between Socialists and Trades Unionists on the single idea of political unity and independence of Labour. This has so far worked well, the two sections having acted 1 )yally together. The Socialists agreed to work loyally with trades unionists who are not Socialists, provided they are prepared to work with Socialists for the common cause of Labour, independent of other political parties. The Conference therefore acted quite consistently in refusing to force Socialism down the throat of any Labour candidate or member of Parliament. Had the amendment been adopted it would have made affiliation to the Labour party tantamount to a declaration of Socialism by each and all the affiliated bodies. It will therefore be clearly understood why the Confer- ence, composed as it was of delegates —the majority of whom were Socialists —rejected the amendment by a majority of ten to one. The resolution put fortvard by the Engineers' Society, which was carried by 514,000 to 460,000 votes, - and which vote, has been so vigorously con- demned by the Liberal and Tory press —was of quite a different character to the one rejected. This resolu- tion was merely a declaration of opinion on the part of the delegates present .at the Conference, and is in no sense binding upon the organizations affiliated to .the Labour party. Trades Unions may dissent from it if they so desire, but so long as it is not imposed as a constitutional test upon affililiated bodies, they need not feel debarred from the party by the result of the vote.

It is not my desire to attempt to minimise the importance of that result, for, althouga it is quite true that a Socialist resolution has been adopted at past Conferences, and by an even greater majority, the conditions have never been quite the same on any previous occasion. This Conference was held after a year of vigorous anti-Socialist propaganda. Never before have the Press and the public been watching so keenly to see how the Conference would act regard- ing the question of Socialism. The resolution was also strongly opposed by Mr. Shackleton, M.P. who represented the non-Socialist section of the delegates. When we consider all these circumstances, and the result of the vote, it proves—at lest to myself, —the continued growth of Socialist opinion amongst the trades unionists.

The statement of a section of the press that " the trades unionists who are not Soei:dists can no longer retain their membership of the Labour party " is not true, although no doubt it is what our opponents would like it to mean. Neither does the vote mean the breaking up of the party. I believe that it will continue to grow, and that ultimately it will embrace Socialism as its object. That however will not come just yet, and in my opinion it does more harm than good to attempt to force Socialism upon , the trades unionists whilst so many of them —although perhaps not opposed to Socialism—have not yet she wn a desire to accept that principle as one of the objects of their trades unions.
Next week I will rebut the charge so often made against Socialists of unfairly exploiting the trade union funds.
A DELEGATE.

div.head: MUNICIPAL COAL SUPPLY.
div.p: MUNICIPAL COAL SUPPLY.

Sir,—l noticed in your column of the Bth instant, ! under the above heading a short contribution bearing the signature of "Liberty." Your correspondent states that the Co-operative Stores have lately embarked on a coal supply. "The Stores " said he "is a democratic institution and as such can be fairly compared to the Wat riugton Cor- poratiOn." Reading on we are farther told th,t on account of the long hours worked in the coal depart- ment two Co-operative employes have transferred their services to private trading concerns, whilst the members of the Stores placing orders for coal can get the same through the Co-operative supply b.v waiting a week or more.

Strange to say, John, this series of so called argu- ments " Liberty " apparently believes "point out the utter fallacy of a municipal coal supply." The modern Co-operative movement has been well described as a system of "glorified shopkseping," for the steadily increasing number of mere dividend hunters amongst its members has introduced a spirit of commercialism directly opposed to the ideals of Robert Owen and the Rochdale Pioneers.

The Co-operative Society (as I understand it) is a syndisiate formed to supply its shareholders (or members) with provisions, clothing, furniture, &c., and the directorate (or executive) who control the business are periodically elected by these shareholders. The activities of the Ca-operative Society are almost exclusively confined to those particular branches of trade from which a direct cash profit can be produced, and their executives and officials have not equal financial resources at their command, neither do they possess the administrative ability, nor can they obtain the comparatively extensive information, that is placed at the disposal of the average county, city, town, urban or rural council. _ _

On the other hand municipalities and local governing bodies generally have, during recent years, in various directions wisely extended their influence with communally beneficial results in every part of the country. Take for example the two humane far-reaching reforms initiated by the Bradford City Council, namely, feeding of necelisitons school-children and the medical inspection of scholars attending the elemental', schools undrr their control. I here invite " Liberty to read carefully the well-compiled official reports explaining in detail the Bradford Education Com- mittee's efforts on these two sncial experiments on child-life. lam certain be will then become con- vinced that no Co-operative Society could se capably and intelligently administer' these pressing reforms as the Bradford City Council have done.

The Warringto'n Corporation now take complete control of the town drainage and scavenging, administer the National system of education in all the local public schools, in addition to discharging the exacting duties connected with the municipal tram service, the gas, water and electric supplies and the public parks. libraries, technical school, museum, &c. Then what feasible objection can possibly be urged against the suggested extension of this well tested principle to the retail distribution of coal amongst 1 the inhabitants of Warrington? I would further point out to " Liberty" that the transference from private enterprise to public control of any business has in the past generally resulted in a substantial improvement of the industrial conditions of its employees and has also, in many instances, been the means of both shortening the hours of labour and increasing the wages of the manual workers engaged therein.

In conclusion Sir, allow me to quote the following stirring words from a speech delivered by Alderman Hoy when Lord Mayor of !..'fanchester: "The expansion of Corporation activity is not likely to diminish in volume. The growth of municipal responsibilities illustrates the drift, and as I believe the irresistible drift of public affairs. Democratic ideal is being worked out through municipalities. Some day men will awake to the immense possibilities of corporate life, and the community will find salvation, not in the patron- age and gifts of the wealthy, but in the combined and intelligent efforts of the people themselves.'
"DEMOS."

What brings the colour to the cheek Of those that suffer and are weak— Whose ailments have but made them crave To be released and in the grave ? What now has given such desire To live again ? you may inquire. Consumption cannot well endure , The strength of Woods' Great Peppermint Cure.—Advt.

div.head: " FAUST" LEGEND.
div.p: THE " FAUST" LEGEND.

That a personage known as Dr. Faust, or Faustus, from whose history the Faust Legend took its rise, actually lived in the earlier part of the lfith century seems beyond doubt. He is spoken of in the writings of contemporaries. Re is said to have been born either at Knittlingen in Wtirtemburg, or at Rods near Weimer. His parents were poor, but the bequest of a wealthy uncle enabled him to study medicine and magio at Cracow. He is described ins letter written in 1507 as Faustus Junior, and as being skilled in necromancy, astrology, magic, chiromancy, and other doubtful sciences. His character appears from general testimony to have been of the worst description. The date of his death is uncertain, but it was not later than 1544, for IJohann Gast, a Protestant theologian, relates that he himself supped with Faust at Basel, where he was attended by a dog and horse that were evidently demons, and further describes his remarkable and, how the devil strangled him, and how his dead body lay constantly on its face on the bier, although turned upwards as often as five times. Another contemporary confirms the account that he died in an inn, during the night, at the hands of his familiar spirit, when his hour had come. Luther is said to have spoken frequently of Faust in conversation, as an illustration of the craft and wickedness of the devil. It has been argued that, as the real Faust called himself Faustus junior, there was an earlier Faust ; there is no record of him however, possibly the name had already become typical. To what extent the Faust Legend takes its rise from the recognition of the elemental struggle between the higher and the lower natures in man—on the one hand the deliberate choice of evil, on the other an unsatisfied aspiration towards the highest good—how far, in short Faust is but a type ; how much is due to the still older conception of a compact with the Evil one: and lastly,l what are its bearings in relation to the conflict between Romanism and Protestantism in Germany at the period of the Reformation, are questions of great interest, but of course, far beyond the scope of the present slight sketch. The first literary version of the Faust story was published in 1587, at Frankfort. It had extra- ordinary popularity and was quickly translated into English, Dutch, French, and Flemish. The English translation is entitled " The Damnable life and Deserved Death of Dr. John Faustus." It was reprinted only a few years ago in an edition edited by Prof. Henry Morley, and published by Routledge. In this remarkable book it is recorded that Faust made a com- pact with the Devil, signing away his soul in return for the services of Mephistopheles for twenty-four years. The fiend supplies him with means, wherewith he and his familiar, Wagner (not the Wagner of Gounod's opera) are able to live in luxury. A few of the necromantic feats recorded in this curious and edifying biography may be mentioned. Faust devours a peasant's load of hay, together with the horse and wagon, produces fresh apples and grapes in January, draws forth wine from a table, and raises from the shades the beautiful Helen of Troy, with wham he afterwards lives, and who bears him a son. The end, as here recorded, is sufficiently awe-inspiring. On the night on which his twenty-four years expired he was in company with a group of Students in a tavern of the village of Ri elk!), near Wittenberg, and to them he made a long address expressing his deer) penitence after which he remained alone in his chamber. At midnight a fearful storm arose, horrible hisses as of a thousand serpents were heard, and for a little while the agonising cries of Faust, with a hollow and suffo- cated sound, but soon all was still. Tr) the morning the floor of the room was found stained with blood, his brains were spattered on the walls, and his body was found outside, the head and every member hanging half torn off.

Other versions of the story quickly appeared, and the enormous extent to which the Faust story has taken hold of the popular imagination may be realised by the fact that there was published in Germany, in IRBS, complete catalogue of Faust literature, in which the number of items given by the bibliographer is two thousand seven hundred and fourteen. From this mass of matter two noble works must be singled ont. (1) The Doctor Faustus of the English dramatist, Marlowe, written about the year 17,89, which however crude, and even puerile in parts, contains 40,11() of the finest dramatic poetry in our language. for instance :
" Was this the faee that lanoch'd a thuu,and ships And burnt the topless towers of Ilium."

div.head: Again : "0 thdu art fairer thin the eveainz air, Clad in the beauty of a thousand stars."
div.p: Again : "0 thdu art fairer thin the eveainz air, Clad in the beauty of a thousand stars."
And the oft quoted :
"Cut is the brannh that might have grown full straight, And barned is Apollo's laurel bough."

(2) The " Fanst " of Goethe (completed in 1831) in which is achieved the transformation of Faustus from a vulgar con;uror into a personification of humanity. It is to Goethe, moreover, thit we owe the exquisite conception of MarguArite (Gretchen.) In more modern poetry we have the" Nfanf,ed " of Byron, the " Paracelsus " of Browning, the " Balder " of Dobell, the" Spiridion "of George S rnd. the " Brand " of Ibsen, thc " TannUnser," of Grisebach ; and in ftction, the" Zanoni " and the " Margrave." of Lord Lytton—all betraying more or less affinity with the typical figure of Faust. The familiar " Golden, Legend " of Longfellow is practically the same story with a happier ending.

div.head: FAUST IN ART.
div.p: FAUST IN ART.

First in importance are the ancient wall paintings in Auerbach's cellar at Leipzig, bearing date 1525, that is to say during the lifetime of the the real Faust. Then there is a well-known engraving by Rembrandt, and others (still older) by von Sichem. Next the illustra- tions to Goethe's " Faust " by Cornelius, Retzsch, Seibertz, Kaulbach, and Kreeling, Under this heading way be included (for brevity's sake) the picturesque drama produced by Henry Irving at the Lyceum Theatre, in 1885, an adaptation of Goethe's play by W. G. Wills.

div.head: FAUST IN MUSIC.
div.p: FAUST IN MUSIC.

In a very useful and interesting series of articles on the Faust Legend, and its musical treatment, published in the Musical Times of 1886, Mr. Frederick Corder enumerates no fewer than thirty-one more or less important compositions founded on the story of Faust. He admits that there may be, and probably are, many more. The most noteworthy are Spohr's opera of " Faust " (1818) ; Lindpainter's (1791-1856) Overture and Incidental Mnsic to Goethe's Faust ; Edward Lassen's (1876) " Music to Goethe's Faust " of which the writer speaks with enthusiasm ; Berlioz's " Faust " (1846) long neglected, but since its production by Charles Halle in 1830, a favourite work with the larger choral societies—Gounod's opera of " Faust " (1859) ; Boito's opera, " Meilstofele " (1868) ; Richard Wagner's " A Faust Orerture " (1339) ; and Liszt's (1811-1886) " A Faust Symphony." Mr. Corder remarks in conclu- sion that no other subject has ever evoked so much interest among musicians as Faust has clone.—ln their hands we may leave him.

div.head: COMPOSER OF "FAUST,'- CHAS. F. GOUNOD.
div.p: THE COMPOSER OF "FAUST,'- CHAS. F. GOUNOD.
I

,„_ I The life of CFI I.RLES FRANCOIS GOUNOD—uniiao those of so many of the greater musicians—does not furnish very much material for the biographer. He was born in Paris, 17th June, 1819, received his early I musical education from his mother, a distinguished pianist, and at the age of 18 entered the Conservatoire,' where three years later he gal ned the Grand Prix ds Rome. Of his residence in Rome his whole career bears traces, for here he chiefly occupied himself with the study of the old masters, especially Palestrina. In 1843 he returned to Paris, visiting Austria and Germany on the way and becoming acquainted with the music of Robert Schumann. In Paris he became organist of the Missions etrangeres and even attended for two years a course of theology, with the intention of taking orders ; later however, he determined to devote himself to music. His first success as a composer was his " Messe Solonelle" produced in 1851. This was followed by his first opera, " Sappho " (1851), by the chorusos to " Ulysse " (1852). by the opera" La Nonne Sanglante " (1854), and by "Le Mhdicin malgr4 lui "(1858). But it was not until 1859 that Gounod, then over 40 years of age, produced the great work that at once established his position in the domain of music. This was "Faust" produced March 19, 1859, at the Theatre Lyrique' with Mme. Miolan-Carvalho as Marguerite. The libretto, founded on Goethe,by Messrs. Barbier and Carr 4, if it gives little of' the spirit of Goethe, is yet admirable as a drama, and beyond praise as an opera book. The first production of the opera in England was at Her Majesty's Theatre, June 11, 1863. Following " Faust " came the operas " Phil4mon at liancis " (1810), " La Reine de Saba "(1862). " Mirelle " (1864), and "Romeo et Juliette" (1967). From 1870 to 1875 Gounod was residing in England, where he lived a retired life, seeming to shrink from public notice, and disdaining public applause ; he appeired, however, at the Philhar- harmonic, the Crystal Palace, and a few other concerts. After his return to France were prodaced the operas " Cinq Mars " (1878), " Polyeucte " (1878), and Le Tribut de Zamora " (1881). In sacred music Gounod has given us in addition to several masses, at least one oratorio of the very highest class, viz. : "The Redemption," proclaimed at the Birmingham Festival, 1882, and followed in 1885 by its sequel " Mors et Vita." Of his smaller works such as "Gallia," his church music, his songs such as , " Nazareth "and " Le Vallon," his " Funeral March of a Marionette," and his " Meditation on a Bach Prelude," the popularity is unqnestiormble. He died at St. Cloud, Oct. 18, 1893. Gounod was a consummate master of the orchestra, in the treatment of which he has originated many beauti-

div.head: LIBRETTO AND MUSIC OF GOUNOD'S "FAUST."
div.p: THE LIBRETTO AND MUSIC OF GOUNOD'S "FAUST."

The following anslysis of the story and music of Gaunod's " Faust " is from -itanisrd ooeras " by Mr. George P. Upton published by Messrs. Fletchinson and Co., to whom we are indebted for permission to reproduce it. The story of the opera follows Geethe's tragedy very closely, and is confined to the first part. It may be briefly told. Faust, an aged German star'ent, satiated with hnrnan knowledge and despairing of his ability to I unravel the secrets of nature, summons the evil spirit Mephistopheles to his assistance, and contracts to give him his soul in exchange for a restoration to youth. Methistopheles effects the transformation, and reveals to him the vision of Marguerite, a beautiful village maiden, with whom Faust at once falls in love. They set out upon their travels and encounter her at the Kerraesse. She has been left by her brother Valentin. ! a soldier, in care of Dame Martha. who proves herself , a careless guardian. Their first meeting is a casual one ; ! but subsequently he finis her in her garden, and with ! the help of the subtle Mephistopheles succeeds in engaging the young girl's affection. Her simple lover, Siebel, is discarded, and his nosegay is thrown away at sight of the jewels with which Faust tempts her. When Valentin retitrns from the wars be learns of her temptation and subsequent ruin. Be challenges the seducer, and in the encounter is slain by the interven- tion of Mephistopheles. Overcome by the horror of her situation, Marguerite becomes insane,' and in her, frenzy kills her child. She is thrown into prison,where Faust and Mephistopheles find her. Faust urges her to fly with them, but she refuses, and places her reliance for salvation upon earnest prayer and sorrow for the wrong she has done. Pleading for forgiveness, she expires; and as Mephistopheles exults at the catestrophe he has wrought, angels appear amid the music of the celestial choirs and hear the sufferer to heaven. The first act is in the nature of a prelude, and opens with a long soliloquy (" Interrogo invano ") by Faust, in which he laments the unsstisfactoriness of life. It is interwoven with delightful snatches of chorus heard behind the scenes, a duet with Mephistopheles (" Ma ii ciel "). and the delicate music accompanying the vision of Marguerite. The second act is contained in a single setting, the Kermesse, in which the chorus plays an important part. In the first scene the choruses of students, soldiers, old men. girls, and matrons are quaintly contrasted, and are full of animation and characteristic color. In the second, Valentin sings a tender song (" 0 sante medaglia") to a medallion of his sister which he wears as a charm. It is followed bye grim and weird drinking- song (" Dio dell' or"), sung by Mephistopheles. The latter then strikes fire from the fountain into his cup, and proposes the health of Marguerite. Valentin springs forward to resent the insult, only to find his sword broken in his hands. The students and soldiers recog- nize the spirit of evil and overcome him by presenting the hilts of their swords in the form of a cross, the scene being accompanied by one of the most effective choruses in the works (" Tu puvi Is spscle, "). The tempter gone, the scene resumes its gayety. and the act closes with one of the most animated and delight- ful of waltz tempos (" Come la brezza.") The third act is the Garden scene, full of fascinating detail, and breathes the very spirit of poetry and music combined in a picture of love which has never been excelled in tenderness and beauty on the operatic stage. Its principal numbers are a short and simple but very beautiful ballad for Siebel (" La parlate d' amor ") ; passionate aria for tenor (" Salve dimora caste e pure") in which Faust greets Marguerite's dwelling ; a double number, which is superb in its contrasts,—the folk-song " C'eri on re di Thule," a plaintive little ballad sung at the spinning wheel by Marguerite", and the bravura jewel-song, " lb ! e' strsno peter, which is the very essence of delicacy and almost childish glee ; the quartet commencing," V'appogiato al braochio mio," which is of striking interest by the independent manner in which the two pairs of voices are treated and com- bined in the close ; and the closing duet (" Semple?) amar ") between Faust and Marguerite, which is replete with tenderness and passion, and closes in strains of almost ecstatic rapture, the fatal end of which is fore- shadowed by the mocking laugh of Mephistopheles breaking in upon its lingering cadennes. The fourth act is known as the Cathedral act, and established Gounod's reputation as a writer of serious music. It opens with a scene for Marguerite, who has been taunted by the girls at the fountain (" N 4190090 eran 14 le crudeli "), in which she laments her sad fate. The scene abruptly changes to the square in front of the cathedral, where the soldiers, Valentin, among them, are returning, to the jubilant though some- what commonplace strains of the march," Deponiam it brandi." As the soldiers retire and Valentin goes in quest of Marguerite, Faust all Mephis- topheles appear before the house, and the latter sings a grotesque and literally infernal serenade (-Tu, che fai -1' addorrnentata. ') Valentin appears and a quarrel ensues, leading up to a spirited trio. Valentin is slain, and with his dying breath pronounces a malediction (" Margherita ! maledetta !") upoa his sister. The scene changes to the church and in wonderful combination me hear the appeals of Marguerite for mercy the taunting voice of the tempter, and the monkish chanting of the" Dies Iris." mingled with the solemn strains of the,organ. The last act is usnally presented in a single scene, the Prison. It takes the form of a terzetto which is worked no with constantly increasing power to a climax of passionate energy, and at last dies away as Marguerite expires. It stand almost alone among effects of this kind in opera. The curtain falls upon a celestial chorus of apotheosis, the vision of the angels, and Mephistopheles cowering in terror before the heavenly messengers.

div.head: PALACE AND HIPPODROME: Sunday Evening Concert.
div.p: PALACE AND HIPPODROME: Sunday Evening Concert.

An early outcome of the recently established Musician's Union in Warrington has been the formation of an orchestra under the conductorship of Mr. Ernest A. Widdop. Under the title of the Palace Symphony Orchestra this new body of instrumentalists made its first public appearance on Sunday evening. The orchestra is yet by no means complete or well-balanced, the preponderance of brass instruments, or at least the disproportionate self-assertiveness of the players in this section, being on Sunday set against the lack of a r due amount of 'cello and viola tone in a way which was I unecessarily prominent. The section of this orchestra which not only did itself justice in performance but appears to be represented by fully competent exectitants was the wood-wind—a matter upon which the new organisation is to be congratulated. In speaking of the manner in which the orchestra played on Sunday evening some allowances muse of course be made. There was as might be expected a noticeable rawness which, perhaps more than anything else, marked inadequate rehearsal. But what seemed to us of greater moment was the manifested fact that the playing of the orchcstra had in it so little of the conductor's personality. We would remind Mr. Widdop that it is quite possible in pieces like the Introduction to the 3rd act of Lohengrin, the " Rural Scenes " (Matt) and the " Leant sans paroles" (Tschaikowsky) to inspire the men under his baton with some individualistic interpretation of these things. Indeed it is necessary that he should do so if the performance is to be marked by any intelligent insight into the composer's meaning. On Sunday evening the various groups'of instrumentalists were far too much left to their own devices with a result distinctly disappointing to the audience. The best thing that the orchestra did was the" II Trova-' tore "selection, while the feeblest was undoubtedly the opening to the Tannhauser march. Mr C. J. Phillips was somewhat unwisely ambitious in choosing Sarasate's " Zigeunerweisen " for an exposition of his ability as a violin soloist. Even in the abridged form in which he attempted it the slow movement was clearly beyond him in the exigency of its demands for a soulfulness on the part of the performer little removed from pro- I found pathos. The brighter movement came more I within Mr. Phillips's limitations and this he played with a praiseworthy approximation to neatness and crispness, and to that high degree of verve which should be its chief characteristic. There was quite a dainty vocal quartet in the persons of Miss A. Woodland. Miss L. Fairhurst, Mr. R. W. Cook and Mr. P. J. George whose singing of " God is a spirit " from Stetadale Bennett's Woman of Samaria ' was the one bright gem of the concert. For this and a similarly testefri rendering of Sullivan's" Yee, though I walk " these four well-matched singers were most deservedly recalled by the audience. Of Miss L. Fairhurst's abilities as a solo vocalist it is unfortunately not possible to speak so highly. That her interpretation of "Abide with me "and of the allied song Nearer my God to Thes " fell short of one's ideal does not prelude our saying that it gave manifest pleasure to the audience who evinced their approval in a most unmistakable way. Bank Quay Tontine Club. The fifth annual dinner in connection with this club was held on Saturday evening at the Bowling Green Hotel. Nearly fifty members partook of an excellent repast prepared by Mrs. Campbell, after which a smoking concert was held in the clubroom, presided over by the president (Bro. H. Alinsbull). During an interval the Secretary (Bro. Roe) gave a resume of last year's work, and intimated that whereas in 1907 the membership was 60 they had now, so early in the year, nearly SO members. Songs were given by Messrs. George Taylor, T. Welsby, H. I. Pidgeon, j. Martin and J. Gorse. Mr. Gorse was the accompanist.

div.head: STOCKTON HEATH TREE PLANTING. Indignation at the Rechnt Outrage. "DESPERADO AND INSIDIOUS VIPER."
div.p: STOCKTON HEATH TREE PLANTING. Indignation at the Rechnt Outrage. "DESPERADO AND INSIDIOUS VIPER."

The second anniversary of Tree Planting Day was celebrated at Stockton Heath on Saturday afternoon when a pnblic meeting was held at the Hall Café, followed by the planting of numerous trees and the unveiling of a commemoration shield on the guard surrounding the Genera Buller tree. The inhabitants of the village had been urged "to show in no uncertain manner their indignation at the work of the miscreant who, under cover of darkness, did the trees so much damage. Stockton Heath surely is not going to allow one person, or two, to turn it from its purpose." Thera was a large attendance at the meeting and if the individual who was responsible for the work of destruction had heard the choice assortment of epithets which were hurled at him he would not have felt flattered. Mr. R. I. Wynne Jones presided and there were also present the Mayor of Warrington (Alderman Smethurst), Mr. C. E. Parker, Dr. Parker. Rev. Canon Stevenson, Rev. C. Harvey Cook, Mr. C, Plinston(chairman of the committee and hon.treasurer),. and Mr. A. Fawcett (hon. secretary). Letters of apology for inability to attend were read from ir.Allan Sykes, Mr. Roger C. Parr, Hon. and Rev. C. F. Cross, airs. W. B. Roberts, Mr. J. J. Whitley. Miss Bainbridge, Mrs. Vere B. Davie, and Alderman Bennett. The last- named wished to join in expressing his detestation of the crime of the tree murderer whose recent acts were quite at variance with every principle of public duty and deserved the strongest condemnation of the whole community. The Chairman, after expressing regret that Mrs. Wynne-Jones was unable to accompany him, said there were very few residents in that township who were not grateful to the committee for the work they had done. There were still fewer who did not sympathize most heartily with them in the cruel outrage perpetrated recently in the malicious mutilation of the trees. He understood the committee proposed to extend their usefulness in the direction of Walton, on the banks of the Ship Canal, and also in the direction of Latchford. Their scheme could not be carried out without money, and he appealed, at a time when their finances were very low,for help to continue their praiseworthy efforts. (Applause.) rhe Mayor of Warrington said when he heard of the dastardly act to the trees he could have said^something strong. (The Rev. Harvey Cook : " So could the parsons," and laughter.) Shortly afterwards he received a postcard on which was written: " If you will send me a piece of bark from one of those trees I will undertake to find the culprit." He (the Mayor) forwarded the postcard to someone interested, but had heard nothing further. He believed the day would come when they would find out, and he hoped the culprit would confess and express publicly his sorrow for what he had done. Nothing, however, would satisfy them except to bring the culprit before a court of justice. (Applause.) Mr. C. E.Parker said the planting of trees was such a simple and cheap method of improving a district that it was well worth doing. They ought to do all they could to increase the love for trees. Trees were his special love and with his own children he tried to i develop that love. He thought the hest way to prevent a repetition of the acts referred to in Stockton Heath was by fostering the love for trees. Interest in plant life and nature was growing, and he trusted the association would extend their field of activity and encourage other districts to form like associations. The garden suburb movement wan undoubtedly one of the first things to receive attention, and he would be glad ; if that association would do what they could to co-operate in the development of the garden suburbs locally. The Rev. Harvey Cook referred to the question from the standpoint of public health, and pointed out that trees, apart from their msthetic and artistic value, had a beneficial effect on the atmosphere. From principles of public health he gave his hearty support to the movement of tree planting and garden city suburbs. Mr. Plinston said it was necessary to appeal for funds to carry on their work. They owed the bank £B, and they were bound to renew forty trees, which would cost at least £lO. incidental expenses amounted to £5. Then they were obliged to put trees in Roman-road, which, with their maintenance for twelve months, would cost £7. So that they required about £3O ; and they

wanted to do the work as quickly as possible. There was a magnificent stretch of country between the Stag Bridge and the Cantilever Bridge, and they wanted to complete their work of planting the banks of the canal ; with shrubs. He believed those banks could be made a scene of perfect loveliness. Towards the cost of that work Messrs. Greenell, Whitley and Co. promised them ' £lO last year and £lO this year • they ljad rebeived £5 from Lady Greenell, £2 from Mrs. Lyon, £1 from Mr. Bindloss, £1 from Mr. Hickman. and several donations from other friends. He appealed to all present to do their utmost to complete the £5O which would be needed to carry out the whole of their work. (Applause.) Dr. Parker then delivered a long speech which created great amusement, being couched in his usual original and high-flown style. After referring to the inauguration of the movement in Victoria- square two years ago and to the visit of General Buller, Dr. Parker •uoved the following resolution "That this meeting of residents of Stockton Heath and district express its e uphatic condemnation of the dastardly act of the person or persons who recently, maliciously and cowardly damaged the trees which were planted by the inhabitants for the purpose of beautifying the district, and, further, expresses deter- mination to do everything possible to bring the culprit or calerits to justice." (Applause.) Continuing, Dr. Parker said after so raneh interest had been shown in the proceedings by gentlemen of public spirit and edu- cation, this impudent desperado, this pest of society, this murderer defied them all and staggered them by the audacity and the enormity of his outrage. The more they rejoiced, the greater their honours, the r more intense became his hate and passion for revenge. And so when the opportune moment arrived, he stole 'forth under cover of the night to perpetrate his crime, and then, when he had first posted his sentinels, the butchery proceeded. What awful venom must rankle in his heart, when far hours that hand neither faltered nor desisted. Tree after tree, a double line of them, two miles in length, was fatally slashed through. And yet, the insidious vipor knew to keep them intact, lest if completely severed, early detection might put too soon a check to the destruction. What course would they adopt to bring the reprobate to justice ? What other crime was necessary to complete the physionomy of the incendiary, and midnight assassin? Why did he not betake himself to some jungle where he would have wild beasts for his companions and not men or hide himself deep in the slums of some densely populated town where the people pined for the sight of a blade of grass. (Applause). But if his malady, as they believed, was an infirmity, not of the body but of the soul, if egotism, spite and hatred of this kind had blasted in him the last vestige of what was human, inflict upon him the retribution of outraged human laws, and vet, in their ruercy,pray that the grace of God might reach his heart,if not too late—if not too late. (Applause.) 4r. J. W. Bouchier seconded the resolution, and said he agreed with Dr. Parker in his indignation. The Committee were not afraid of criticism or legitimate opposition so long as it was fair and outspoken, but to cut the trees in the manner they had was nu-English. The resolution was carried unanimously; and a vote of thanks was passed to the Chairman on the proposi- tion of Mr. W. H. J. Jenkins, seconded by Mr. T. Baxter.

After the meeting the company proceeded to the Buller tree, where Mrs. Parker, wife of Dr. Pirker, unveiled a shield affixed to the guard and which bore the follow- -1 ing words : "This tree was planted on 21st February, 1907, by General Sir Redvers Boller, V.C., on the occasion of his visit to Warrington to unveil the memorial to Colonel O'Leary and his brave comrades 1 who fell in the South African War. Semper fidelis." Afterwards trees were planted in Victoria Square by , the ;Mayoress of Warrington and Mrs. Henry Roberts, , and in Old London-road by Mrs. T. Baxter, Mrs. Grant, Miss Clarke, Miss Joan Greenall, Miss Josselyne ; the Misses Rathbone, Vernon and Marsh, and Master Walter Mather ; Miss Thom McDermid ; the Misses Gertie Bate, Cissie Twiss and Florrie Bennett ; Miss May. White; and Master Kenneth Woodcock.

Warrington Boy Sent to Reformatory. At the Warrington Police Court, on Thurday, John Clare, of Litton's-row, pleaded guilty to stealing is. 6d. from the till of William Yates, of Knuteford- road, on the 12th inst. The Chief Constable said it would be in the interest of the boy and the publin if he were sent to a reformatory.— The mahistrates com- mitted the boy to Kerrison Reformatory until he was nineteen years of age.
OUR LOCAL CHURCHES.
Legh-street Primitive .Methodist Church.

The anniversary sermons in connection with the above place of worship were held on Sunday when two powerful sermons were preached by the Rev. J. B. Buglass to good congregations. In the afternoon a musical service was given by the choir and friends. Miss E. Taylor (soprano) sang " Entreat rue not to leave thee " (Gounocl) and" Come unto Me," her clear, sweet voice, and perfect intonation being pleasing to listen to. Miss S'. Barnes gave much pleasure in her splendid rendering of the solos "Ave Marie " and We shall meet." Mr. W. H. Booth (tenor) was very successful in "The Psalm Divine " and " My hope is in the Everlasting," the latter especially being later- prated in a truly artistic manner. Mr. J.W.Warburt on was happy in his selection of " Bring forth the best robe" (" Prodigal son," Sullivan) and "Father Eternal" which were well suited to his baritone voice and to which he did full justice. The choir, conducted by Mr. A. Spruce, rendered the anthems " Go when the morning shineth " (Lace), " Rock of Ages (Buck) (the solo in the latter being feelingly sung by Miss A. Woodland) and the chorus " Gloria " (Mozart) with good taste and expression. At the evening service the choir also gave a fine rendering of Woodward's beautiful anthem "The Radiant Morn,"which VMS much enjoyed, Mr. A. W. Clatworthy very creditably acoompanied all the services.

A Social Sunday Evening Hour at Wycliff e. At Wycliffe Church last Sunday evening the Rev. J. Yonge preached especially to young people on" What to flee, what to follow, and the best company in which to be found," the text being, " Flee youthful lusts, but follow righteousness, faith, love, peace, with them that call on the Lord out of a pure heart." He spoke of the text as St. Paul's offer of a competition,or challenge to a pursuit, which he commended as at any rate a very much better thing than some of those numerous competitions so popular in the present day. He ques- tioned the wisdom of those competitions which, as in the case of" Limericks " offered the chance of a large money prize upon the outlay of a small coin, sod the effort of a ready wit. This appeared to him to be simple gambling, inducing numbers of young people Ito waste time needed for better use, and to expend small sums very frequently which amounted in the total to more than they could well afford to throw away. He warned his hearers against indulging in such fortuitous methods of gaining money. He then proceeded to urge the Apostle's advice that all perilous practices and dispositions should be resolutely abandoned and all the effort of the life devotel to the pursuit of character, and of conduct, which could be influential for good. He closed by advocating the wisdom of young people cherishing their early religious associations of Church and school, and religious observance of Sunday.—After the service a " Social hour " was greatly enjoyed by a company which crowded the Memorial Hall. An informal programme was furnished by members of the Young People's Society: Sacred songs were contributed by Miss Griffiths " ! Divine Redeemer," Miss Armstrong " Giver of Life," and Mr. W. J. Barnes " Dream of Paradise." A violin and piano duet was given by Mr. T. F. Wallington and Mr. W. H. Paytor. Miss Jessie Farrar and Miss Ethel Atkinson ably accompanied the songs. Tea, coffee and biscuits were handed round. The hour was closed by the evening hymn, " Sun of my soul," brief prayer and benediction, by the Pastor. Every one present appeared much gratified by the new departure. It is proposed to hold a similar social hour on one of the Sunday evenings in March, and to renew such occasions in the early autumn. Opportunity is thus afforded of a profitable use of a Sunday evening hour and of promoting social fellowship among the people.

Taylor was the accom- panist. Master J. Thompson proposed a vote of thanks to Mr. Podmore, and the artistes, which was seconded by Miss Edith Powell and carried with acclamation. div.head: BRAVERY.
div.p: BRAVERY.

A little ragged boy was once found on board an outward-bound ship that had left port some days. He was brought to the first mate and asked to point out the cheat who had smuggled him on board. The boy replied that his step- father did it as he could not afford to keep him, and so desired to np.d him to a rich aunt abroad. The mate did not believe this story, in spite of the boy's innocent face, for he had heard similar tales before that were not true. He thought the sailors had plotted to help him away, so he dealt hardly towards him repeatedly, and called him bad names. This went on day by day, but in spite of all the boy could not be got to blame the sailors. At last, the mate, who was tired of the boy's story, took him by the throat and dragged him up to the fore-deck. There he pointed to the highest mast, and told the boy that he should hang there in ten minutes unless he told a true tale. People on board gathered round, and in the midst knelt the little boy, while the mate stood in front to take the time. It was one of the finest sights, said a witness, that he ever saw, to see the pale wasted face of that noble boy as he resolved to meet death sooner than lie. As soon as eight' minutes had gone the mate told him that he had only two minutes more to live; he advised him to tell a true story if he wanted to save his life. The boy only answered, "I cannot lie; I should like to pray." The mate nodded his head, turned pale, and shook like a reed in the wind. And there the little fellow knelt, and begged that God might receive him if he died. The scene that next took place touched the hearts of the passengers. The mate sprang for- ward and hugged the boy to his breast. He blessed him and told him that he at last believed his story, and that while he lived he should not want a friend. DORIS TALBOT.

div.head: CHILDREN OF JAPAN.
div.p: CHILDREN OF JAPAN.

You funny little Japanese, I wonder if you're taught To say "No, thank you and "Yes, please," As all good children ought. I hope in far-away Japan You never say "I sha'n't," But always use "I will" and "can't"; I wonder if you ever tear Your coloured pinafores' Or when in temper ever dare To bang and slam the doors. If not, I think in far Japan There must be children who Behave indeed much better than Some English children do. DAISY CAPP.

div.head: ". DREAMS."
div.p: ". DREAMS."

A friend in town who is greatly interested in Sunday, school work amongst the poorest portion of the poptlation, one Sunday, having a class of boys mostly attired in very dilapidated habili- ments, had as the subject of his lesson "Joseph's Dream." In the course of the lesson be was prompted to elicit from his class a definition of a dream. Ultimately, a little ragged urchin of evident Hibernian origin put up his hand as an evidence of his dtsire to pro- pound his definition, and then stated that "A drame is a niagic-lanthon in the head showing picturs whin yer slapin', which ye remimber whin ye waken." L. ANDREWS.
DANDELION, TELL ME TRUE. Dandelion, tell me true: • Does my mother need met

If I blow your fuzzy hair, Thrice I find your head is bare, Home. the sign shall lead me. Dandelion, tell me true: Is my mother grieving? How I long to stay and play In the meadow, if I may; Say, must I be leaving/ Dandelion, tell me true: Does my -mother worry? Blow, and blow, and blow again; Little fuzzies still remain, So I need not hurry. GWENDOLINE KIVELL.
IIMALS AT CHURCH.
When aniiTnaiS"Tri;ide-pia-c-e; of worship they are apt to create considerable comternation amongst the worshippers, who do not find their presence by any means helpful to them in their devotions.

Quite recently, at Broughton Astley Chunh, some four or five miles from Leiceste2, a con- gregation was disturbed by the sudden appear- ance of a fox in the sacred building. 'I •:,e occasion was an intercession service on hchalf of our soldiers in .South Africa; and when Reynard dashed into the church he was quickly followed by the hounds, which had caused him to seek sanctuary there. The worshippers were saved what would have been the unique spectacle of a fox hunt in a place of worship, for the hounds quickly seized the fugitive, and despatched him before leaving the edifice. It is hardly likely, under the cir- cumstances, that any of the field were "in at the death "—to quote the language of the hunt. On the Continent, congregations ha.ve been disturbed by thetintrusion of animals. Not long since, that experience befell the worshippers at the little village church of Arles-sur-Teche, iii the neighbourhood of Perpignan, the intruder being a bull, which had been reserved for a bull- fight that was to take place at a forthcoming village fate. It had somehow broken out of its temporary abode, and its entry into the church creat9d the greatest confusion. While the priest sought shelter in the sacristy, his faithful flock be came panic-stricken, women screaming and fainting, and the men climbing the pillars and creeping under the pews in their scrambles for safety. The beast, however, disdained to notice them, and proceeding along the aisle made its way to the altar, and after sniffing at the articles on it, returned to the aisle and lay down quietly to rest. Even then, a considerable time elapsed before anybody could muster up sufficient courage to creep out of church and seek , assistance.

One man finally did this, however, and the hull's keepers arrived on the scene and led the animal away. On one occasion a monkey took possession of St. Stephen's Church, Hampstead, where, for some time, it baffled all efforts to effect its capture. It wandered about from ground floor to belfry, and out into the churchyard and back again, 'without the slightest difficulty, its presence first becoming known to the cleaner of the church.

Finding that it had been detected, the agile animal quiokly ascended the tower, and making its way out through an aperture in the roof, took up a position on a ledge, from wllich it would have been impossible to dislodge it. Where it came from and what ultimately became of it the present writer is not able to say. The other day there was quite a startling in- cident at a place of worship in the United States —the Dunkard Church, in Highland County, Ohio. A most devout member of the congrega- tion was engaged in offering up a fervent prayer when it was observed that a large black snake was wriggling about the church. It did not escape the notice of the praying member, who forthwith rose from his knees. seized a club, and dealing the reptile several blows killed it .on the spot. _ _ _

This accomplished, he resumed his prayer. which was brought to a conclusion without further interruption. Rats are sometimes unwelcome visitors at churches, where they have been known to create no small amount of trouble. Once during Uhf. morning service at Green Lanes Wesleyan Church, North London, a very large rat put iv an appearance, keeping the congregation for some time in a state of great uneasiness.. .

..... _ _ Then it temporarily vanished, reappearing to- wards the end of the service and resithliag its gambols from pew to pew. Finally, the iircdr became so annoying to the worshippers lr dog was brought on the scene, and an exig chase ensued.

Pursued over the seats, the fugitive took refuge beneath the communion-table, Where it was coon captured by its canine foe. The rash rodent's revels having thus been brought to an end, the congregation breathed more freely. Nothing could be much more disconcerting to the average lady worshipper than to find her ielf in close proximity to a mouse. The effect Produced on the members of the fair sex at the Congregational Church at Buckingham. one Sunday evening, by the presence of a number of young mice, which were running about the pews, can therefore be easily imagined. As the nimble little animals made their way from pew to pew, a nervous rustling of dresses ensued, though—to their credit be it said—none of the ladies either screamed or fainted. The situation, however, proved a great deal too much for the gravity of the younger males present, who it is much to be feared paid but little attention to the service after the mice made their presence known. And the ladies were not sorry when it came to a close
CATERPILLARS' RASH.

Caterpillars are mostly covered with short hairs or bristles. They may crawl ov'er one's skin without the slightest inconvenience, but immediately on being handled these bristles break off and stick in the skin, and the more one tries to brush them off the more they spread. The greatest offender is the larva of the "brown-tailed moth" found in the early part of June on the hawthorn. The rash these bristles cause sometimes lasts for over a week. FOLLOWED THE VAN. .

A wise old black cat watched every article of furniture taken from his old home, and when the last pantechnicon left and the door was finally closed, he followed the van quite resignedly, and after a thorough search of the new house he settled down in his new quarters as though he had been there all his life.
" What is an anecdote, Johnny?" asked the teacher. . .
"A short, funny tale,'' answered the little fellow.

"That's right," said the teacher. "Now. Johnny, you may write a eentence on the black- board containing the word." Johnny hesitated a moment and then wrote this: "A. rabbit has four legs and one anecdote.'"

div.head: AN INTELLIGENT GULL.
div.p: AN INTELLIGENT GULL.

A gull which was on the grass near some ornamental water suddenly pounced on a sparrow close by and picked it up in his beak. Finding that his captive ,was rather too much for him, the gull ran to the water's edge, Calmly held the sparrow under the water till it was drowned and then ate it!

Many fish can produce musical Sounds. The .red gurnard has earned the name of seacock from the crowing noise which it makes, while another species is called the piper. Others have sound-producing apparatus, consisting of small, movable bones, which can be made to produce a sharp rattle. The curious " drumming " made by the Mediterranean fish known as the maigre can be heard from a depth of thirty fathoms.

div.p: TFIE NORTHERN LEAGUE.

Hull K. Rovers ... 0 2 6 Leeds* Hunslet 4 1 11 Wakefield T.* ... 0 0 0 Bradford N Hal i fax Batley* Broughton Ran. ... 2 725 Merthyr Tydvil 0 1 3 Salford Widnes* 0 9 6 Dewsbury 0 2 6 Wigan* Barrow* 1 2 8 Runcorn Oldham* St. Helens 1 1 5 Ebbw Vale* ... 0 1 3 York* Warrington v. Wigan.

The Warrington men journeyed to Wigan on Saturday with a fairly strong team, though Lees, Thomas, Taylor and Jenkins were all absentees. Wigan were short of Jenkins and Leytham. After a wet morning, fine weather prevailed, and 10,000 spectators witnessed the match. The ground was very soft and spoiled combined play. Both teams being in the running for the South- West Lancashire Championship lent extra interest, and the victory of Wigan secured them the trophy. Teams : Warrington: Tilley, back ; Fish, Isherwood, Dicken- son, and Watkins three-quarters ; Brooks and Lloyd, half backs ; Jenkins, Shugars, Harmer, Naylor, Belton, and Jolley, forwards. Wigan: Sharrock, back ; Creevey, T. Thomas, Treharne, and Miller, three-quarters ; David and Gleave, half backs ; Silcock, Cheetham, Barton, Rains. dale, Wilcock, and Brookes, forwards. Referee. Mr. F. Renton (Huuslet.) 'touch-judges, Messrs. W. H. Cawley (Runcorn) and D. Thompson (Preston). Cheatham started for Wigan and David, Wigan's recent capture, early demonstrated that he was in rare form, for judicious punting caused Warrington to fall back. Tilley, however, cleared out the invaders, and smart work by Brooks and Dickenson was the means of Sharrock being called. Wigan again forced matters, and after Treharne and David had tried to break through, the latter secured near the line, and though twirled, suooeeded in grounding for Creevey to give his side a five points' lead. Warrington did not relax their energies on resuming, and Wigan had a hard task to keep the opposition out, Jenkins, Isherwood, and Fish all making attempts to cross. Jolley was hurt and com- pelled to retire. Respective dribbles by Fish and Miller harassed the defence, and eventually the ball was forced over the Warrington line, and in the general rush for possession Wilcock scored a try. Warrington again rallied, and after good work between Lloyd, Isherwood and Brooks, Fish got possession and cleverly eluded several of the opposition, scoring far out. Wigan res-, ponded, and Cheetham scored, Creevey missing the goal- kick. At half-time Wigan led by 11 points to three. Re-starting, Tilley was early called upon to defend, which he did in admirable fashion. By easy stages Warrington assumed a menacing position, and after Fish had defeated Creevey, passing between Watkin, Dickenson, and Isherwood gave the " Wirepullers " a firm footing in the Wigan quarters. The visitors were badly fouled when their prospects of a score were exceptionally bright, and from the penalty Brooks succeeded in reducing some of the leeway. In the last stages Watkin dribbled splendidly from half-way, only to be defeated on the line by Sharrock, whilst a clever run by Fish gave Isherwood an opportunity in the last moment. He was, however, pushed into touch near the "tomer, and the whistle soon after sounded for " no-side." Result : Wigan one goal three tries (11 points), Warrington one goal one try (five points).
