WARRINGTON "A" BEATEN AT HOME.

The match with Wigan " A " on Saturday attracted one of the largest" gates " at a Combination match seen at Wilderspool this season. The issue of the game was of the utmost importance to the competing teams, for both are running a close race for Championship honours. The visitors' side was an exceptionally strong one, but the Warrington combination was weakened by the absence of such players as Landor, Cartwright, and Harris. Warrington had the advantage of a stiff breeze during the first half, and, Wigan starting, the visitors soon swarmed round the pavilion goal, and the ball was taken over. The try was negatived through off-side play, and immediately after Warrington forced matters at the Wigan end, where Coulthard was seen to advantage. Jordan dribbled well, and the Wigan custodian was forced to kick over his own line to save disaster. From the ensuing , scrimmage Heath charged a kick and scored near the corner. Brilliant passing by the Wigan backs caused the local defence much anxiety, and, after a series of attempts, Greenwood put on a try after a fine effort by Green, Coulthard giving his side the lead with a neatly- placed goal. Warrington again raised the siege, and clever work by Daintith culminated in Jordan dropping a goal near the interval, so that the teams crossed over each claiming five points. Turning round, Warrington, by the aid of robust forward work, found Coulthard much employment. Bullen, however, put on the finishing touch to a round of passing, and punting past Knight, soon showed the opposition a clean pair of heels. Wigan notched another try, the result of good forward work,after which the play became"scrappy",and one of the visitors was ordered to retire. Knight was badly hurt and carried off. Coulthard placed a penalty goal. Warrington made an effort near the close, and Daintith scored for Forster to place a goal. Final : Wigan, two goals, three tries (13 points), Warrington, two goals two tries (10 points).

div.head: JUNIOR LIBERALS. Rev. John YWig—e-s. Lecture on
div.p: JUNIOR LIBERALS. Rev. John YWig—e-s. Lecture on
Gladstone.

I At the meeting of the Warrington Junior Liberal Association on Monday evening the Rev. John Yonge ' gave a paper on "The Right Hon. W. E. Gladstone." Councillor Hawthorn presided over a good attendance. , Mr. Yonge said the lecture was really a sketch drawn ! from Morley's " Life of Gladstone," and was biographical more than it was political : an attempt to describe a high-minded, strenuous and brilliant life which had held a supreme place in the annals of the last century, and which bad made a great deal of very widely influential history. Any attempt to present Gladstone's life could not be less than interesting and useful to the younger Liberals of our day—interesting because his great career presented so fine an example of heroic devotion to conviction of truth and right, and useful because that career suggested lines of political thought and enterprise along which the cause of Liberalism must persevere in the future more ardently than ever. Mr. Yonge then gave a most interesting sketch of the life of " The Grand Old Man." He said it was simply marvellous to read the records of Gladstone's capacities for work. They conveyed one long reproof to the ordinary man—whether junior or senior. 'fhe reading he did,rand the writing—the meetings he spoke at; the length of his Parliamentary speeches 2,3, 4, 5 hours—orations upon which the whole House used to hang in breath- less interest. It might be well, said Mr. Yonge, to make a brief allusion to what they might imagine Mr. Gladstone's attitude, especially in the Education ques- tion,vvould have been had he still been alive. Anyone re- calling him in the present controversy would have small difficulty in defining his rel ation to it. They could con- jeoture what he would be likely to say to the House of Lords and to the country. We had a strong Liberal Government, backed by a tremendous majority in the House of Commons and in the nation, checked and thwarted by an impracticable Upper House dominated on this matter by an imperious episcopal bench. The Church once more revealed itself less as the friend of I the people than as the jealous conservator of its own privileges. Might they not believe that Gladstone would be likely to say at this juncture what he did say in a letter to one of his sons in April 1865 concerning the question of Church Rate Abolition. That, of course, was resisted by the Church. He said : "It is some- times necessary in politics to make surrenders of what if not surrendered, will be wrested from us. And it is very wise, when a necessity of this kind is approaching to anticipate it while it is yet a good way off; for then concession begets gratitude, and often brings a return. The kind of concession which is really mischievous is just that which is made under terror and extreme pressure ; and unhappily this has been the kind of concession which for more than 200 years, it has been the fashion of men who call (and yam really think) themselves friends of the Church to make. I believe it would be a wise concession, upon grounds merely political, for the Church of England to have the law of Church rates abolished in all cases where it places her in fretting conflict with the dissenting bodies. I am convinced that the only hope of making it possible for her to dis- charge her high office as stewardess of divine truth is to deal tenderly and gently with all the points at which her external privileges grate upon the feelings of that unhappily large portion of the community who have almost ceased in any sense to care for her. This is a principle of broad application, broader far than the mere question of Church rates." They could have little doubt as to where Gladstone would be found to-day if he were still upon this earthly scene. He would have encouraged the party of progress to face and fight the aristocratic heirs of privilege, and the believers in and upholders of a tyrannical prelacy, in their present conspiracy to put back the clock and to rivet afresh the chains of bondage upon the people's will. " Liberals and especially Free Church- men " continued Mr. Yonge " must look upon the present position as one of glorious opportunity. They must be prepared for the time to accept unflinchingly all the aspersions which the bitter zeal, of State Church- men may hurl at them. Let them objurgate by what- ever name they please. Let them go on fabricating fallacious charges against motives and policies. Let them continue to show their ignorance alike of fact and truth in every pul,lic demonstration they fnake. It pleases them to pose as the true friends of the parent and the child—as the only popular educationists which the country ever possessed until 1870 ! The nation can afford to smile at their ingenious fancy and their parental solicitude. But it knows its history and it is going to have its freedom soon. Then when the con- troversy about the schools is over and when the question of ecclesiastical State establishments is finally disposed of, Ephriam shal: no longer envylJudab, or Judah vex Ephraim, and Anglican, Roman, Evangelical and Rationalist will no longer be in the embitterment of strife."

The CIIAIGAIAN said they were all indebted to Mr. Yonge for the interesting paper he had just delivered. It was an inspiration to them as young Liberals to listen to a paper of that description, and he was sure Mr. Yonge bad done full justice to the life of Glad- stone. (Hear, hear.) Mr. E. ENGLAND said be first saw Mr. Gladstone at Market Gate in 1868, when he was being driven to the Royal Court Theatre in Rylands-street—then the Public Hall—when he addressed the electors of ,outhLancashire but he(Mr.England did not have the privilege of hearing Mr. Gladstone speak. He endorsed all that the Chair- man had said.

Mr. }ono proposed a vote of thanks to Mr. Yonge for the interesting lecture he had given them. • Mr. JONES seconded, and the motion was carried unanimously. Mr. YotsoE, in reply, said it was a very great source of gratification to come amongst them. They must get ready for the next election, because if they wanted to win they would have to fight very hard, as there VMS another party in the town who meant to have a repre- sentative at the next election.

div.head: Town Ball, Warrington, Feb. 21st, 1909.
div.p: Town Ball, Warrington, Feb. 21st, 1909.

Is Interest Robbery Sir.—Mr. Kettle appears to have got to the end of his argument and takes refuge in abusing mine. He again states it is illogical and fails to show why. He styles my description of capital as " stored toil and anconsumed labour" as " Isere sentimental phrases which are humbug in a question of this kind. As to whether I (Mr. K.) agree with the borrower refusing to pay for the loan of the spade I refuse to say, 9r,c." Refusing to answer an argument and taking cover in abusing it is a method as cheap as it is unworthy. " Illogical—sentimental phrases—humbug "may appear to Mr. Kettle smart but they carry no conviction to those who desire to find the truth. Strange to say, Mr. Kettle gives himself away in the following sentence "To think out and make a spade involves both mental and manual labour, and as such is entitled to the award of ability and generally gets it, sometimes snore so. Under our present system this reward usually takes the form of royalty, rent, or share of profits, and it is a recognized fact that a service has been rendered by labour which must be paid for." This is just what I have been arguing for all along, and as Mr. Kettle admits this title to reward he admits my whole conten- tion, where then is there any utility in further corres- pondence? The only difference left is that what I call interest, Mr. Kettle calls " royalty, rent, or share of profits." He admits that the worker who thus stores his labour is entitled to the reward, but gives the reward a different name. The difference between us is reduced to the difference between tweedledee and tweedledum. But I contend that the term interest is the proper one to use in this connection. The payment for borrowed capital (stored labour) is always spoken of as interest by every writer on economics whether he be a Socialist or no. To call this, say, rent is a misuse of terms which only leads to confusion. It seems so me that if this controversy is to lead to any conclusion we will have to go back to where we ought to have started and define the meanings of the i terms we employ. I do not wish to force my defini- tions on Mr. Kettle. I am willing to adopt his if he will give them, as long as they clearly differentiate one factor from another, but 'claim that in dealing with economics we ought to adopt the generally accepted definitions used by all writers on this subject. Mr. Kettle while seeming to admit the justice of the reward to the maker of the spade denies it to the man who changes his labour product into money and lends it through a bank. Thus while the maker of the spade is, according to Mr. Kettle, entitled to royalty, rent, or share of profit when he lends it direct ; if under our present system he sells his spades, banks the cash, and the banker lends the cash to a third party who exchanges it for a plough, then the original maker of the spade becomes a " a robber " if he gets interest through the bank instead of directly from the user of the capital— Strange ! ! . CHARLES E. PARKER. Penketh, February ISth, 190 S.

div.head: Warrington Bridge.
div.p: Warrington Bridge.

Sir,—Will you allow us a little of your space to meet some of the remarks recently made about us and to state, as simply and shortly as we can, the position we have taken up ? Our business at Mersey Mills is entirely dependent on water carriage; without the economies this gives us the Mill could not be carried on at a profit. This Mill was rebuilt in 1863,at a very heavy cost, and is one of the heaviest ratepayers in the town. We have had to spend large sums to defend our rights to this water carriage. Warrington Bridge,as it now is, forms a very dangerous and difficult bar to all vessels ; it lies in a sharp bend of the river, where the currents are particularly strong and only by most skilful handling is it possible to pass vessels under its narrow arch during certain conditions of the river. The current at this point is in our opinion more difficult than it used to be before the new river diversion was cut at Arpley and before Howley weir wts altered by inserting tilting i sluices. Any alteration of the bridge which will make the navigation of the river more difficult and dangerous than it now is, may,and probably will, be a fatal blow to our business; we are absolutely bound to oppose such a suggestion to the very utmost of our power. You may take our word for it that widening the bridge in the way now proposed will most seriously add to the danger and difficulty of navigation. If your readers will try to imagine what it means to run a boat, such as one of ours, under the bridge, we cannot help thinking they will agree with us. You must remember that a boat has extremely little clearance between the piers of the arch, that she must keep a fair head of steam to force her against the strong current, that as she emerges she meets a cross current of great strength tending to throw her across the piers, this has happened to us already, and she has to undertake this ,ticklish bit of steering and navigation with her funnel dropped back and with the helmsman half blinded and smothered in smoke. Every extra second the funnel has to be down increases the difficulties enormously. This is but one point ; there are others, but perhaps we have said enough to show that we are not talking with- out reason. The Corporation are themselves the owners of the stone wharf, of Bishops wharf, and have recently had to acquire a good lot of property on the Latchford side of the river, east of Bridge-street. If they injure the navigation they do themselves a considerable hurt. It is not likely that Bishops wharf will command a good rent if it is difficult and dangerous to get boats to it. If their stone wharf is useless for vessels every ton of road metal .will cost them dearer. By the united action of the Corporation and traders we have secured a river with 8 feet depth at low water, practi- cally a dock, and now the Corporation are going to cut off a large slice of this dock and render its water frontage valueless. The town wants a better bridge and we do not in the least desire to stop this very reasonable wish. The new bridge would benefit us personally no more than any other townspeople, and we have said from the start that if a new bridge is built, having regard not only to those who go over it, but also to those who have a right ; to go under it, we will help all in our power. We offered £l,OOO if the bridge were so built that not only , would the roadway and footwalks upon it he widened, but that also the waterway underneath be also widenecli We do not consider we were under the smallest obliga- tion to make this oiler, as the Corporation have no right to interfere in the smallest way with our navig- able channel, or tb make it the least bit more difficult I than it is now, but with a cordial wish to act well towards our native town, aud in the hope it would induce the Town Council to adopt a really thorough- going scheme. The present suggestion is, at the best, a makeshift. It cannot answer its purpose for more than a short time, and the money spent upon it will really be wasted.—Yours faithfully, JAMES FAIRCLOUGH ,ch SONS. LTD. Mersey Mills, . Warrington, Feb. 20th, 1908.

div.head: MR. P. H. CROSFIELD, M.P. The Illuminated Address from arrington Liberals.
div.p: MR. P. H. CROSFIELD, M.P. The Illuminated Address from arrington Liberals.

The illuminated address presented to Mr. A. 11. Crosfield, M.P. by the Liberals of Warrington on the occasion of his marriage, has been completed and is I now on view in the shop window of Mr. T. Birtles, Sankey-street. It is a most artistic production and ' reflects the greatest credit upon Mr. E. A. Sanders who has carried out the work. The address is executed entirely in water colours and old gold and is beauti- fully designed. At the top appears the dove of love I holding the olive branch of peace and overlooking the eye of watchfulness from which stream forth rays of sunlight, depicting future happiness and prosperity. In the top corners are the monograms A.H.C. and D.O and in the bottom corner are clasped hands to represent greeting. The inner border of the address is in the style of a chain and the outer border is worked in the form of a pillar, symbolical at strength. There is also some choice ornamentation, and Mr. Sanders is to be complimented upon the appropriate- ness of the complete design and the happy way in which he has carried it into effect. The lettering is in the old English style. The signatories to the address are : Charles E. Parker, presideht ; David Tinnion, chairman ; Thomas Pemberton, hon .treasurer ; James T.Locker,hon.secretary ; John Wilkinsonelames Evans,Peter Peacock,W.FurnessJ.Green Chappell,John Worrall, C.Jackson Holmes,W. div.head: TEMPERANCE REFORM. ALLIANCE ifigYING AT THE PARR HALL.
div.p: TEMPERANCE REFORM. ALLIANCE ifigYING AT THE PARR HALL.
Speeches by the Rev. Canon Hicks and Mr. T. H. Sloan, M.P.

A public meeting promoted by the 'United Kingdom Alliance in support of temperance reform was held in the Parr Hall on Wednesday evening. There was a fairly large and representative gathering. Mr. James Dodds presided and was supported on the platform by the Rev. Canon Hicks. of Manchester, Mr. T. H. SlOlO, Conservative M.P. for Belfast, and Mrs. Sloane, Mrs. Dodds, Mrs. Simpson, Revs, W. Bracecamp, J. Yonge, J. P. Matthews, C. Harvey Cook, W. Msllor, J. B. Buglass, Councillors Barton and Skelland, Messrs. C. E. Parker, T. Dale, D. Hodge, E. Boreland and I others.

The CHAIRMAN said he had been a member of the U.E.A. for over forty years—(applause)—so that he need not say he was entirely in accord with its objects and with the resolution which would be submitted. He had received the following telegram from Captain Richard Rigg, who was announced to speak :—" Deeply regret called North. 'Urgent private business. Cannot come to-night. Warmly appreciate your kind invite- tion.—R IG G." He was glad to say their revered friend Canon Hicks was with them—(applause)--and he was sure that in itself was gratifying to them all. They had also to bear Mr. Sloan, M.P.—(applause)—and with such a competent and powerful deputation he anticipated they would have a very good meeting although he was sorry the attendance was not larger. He had received letters regretting inability to attend from the Revs. F. Vaughan and S. Pitt and several others.

In the course of his letter the Rev. S. Pitt said : V ill allow me to say how much I feel the need , of rallying all the available forces of temperance in Warrinston at the present moment. The drink traffic is organised to the utmost. It has one hundred and twenty committee rooms in full and constant activity,to say nothing of off-licences.On the other hand the temper- ance forces are scattered and inefficient. lam con- vinced that there is a powerful sentiment in the Borough comprising many shades of opinion which might if it could be brought together, do something to improve matters." The Rev. F. Vaughan wrote :—" My attitude on this national question is easily defined. To me there can be but one attitude for the Christian Church,viz.,that of uncompromising hostility towards a trade which,despite its present legal status is, nevertheless, the greatest national foe. It is a matter of much thankfulness that at last the leaders of public opinion are pronouncing against the present licensing system as unjust in many ways, and it is to be hoped that such support will be given to the present Government that much needed legislation may be at once secured. I believe that when the whole Christian Church will dare to face tkis question with clean hands and declare that a man- destroying, God-dishonouring traffic must cease, that end will be secured."

div.head: RESOLUTION.
div.p: THE RESOLUTION.

The Rev. J. F. MATTHEWS moved the following resolution :—"That this meeting thanks the Government for the promise in the King's Speech of a Bill to amend the law of licensing in England and Wales, and trusts that the measure shall include among other reforms : (1) A short time limit to the compensation clauses of the Licensing Act of 1904 ; (2) restoration and exten- sion of discretionary powers of the local licensing authority, bringing every kind of licences under magis- terial control ; (3) provisions for conferring upon the inhabitants of every locality the power to prevent by direct popular vote not only the issue of new licences but also the renewal of existing licences as soon as the vested interest set up by the Act of 1904 has been terminated." He said he was not quite sure whether resolutions did them very much good. He had had an uneasy feeling for some years that they had "resoluted," as the Americans said, and " resoluted " until Govern- ments and Cabinets were sick and tired of their resolu- tions and took precious little notice of them. He was not sure also that he had not within the last fifteen or sixteen years lost faith in the promises of Governments to do what they required on matters connected with temperance and licensing reform. He was not quite sure that he trusted the Liberal party—(laughter)—to do all that one would like to see them do, but at any rate they must do the Government the justice of supposing they intended in this case real and serious business. (Hear, hear.) In support of this statement Mr. Matthews quoted speeches by the Premier and Mr. D.Lloyd-George, M.P. There was only one other man in the Cabinet whose opinion on temperance matters would weigh very much with him, and that was Mr. Churchill. If they had those three men on their side—and he thought they had—they had reason to believe that the Government meant something serious. He would gladly welcome anything that would in the least degree curtail the influence of the drink traffie, so he was prepared for as little as the present Government might give and he would gladly accept it, but he was prepared for as much more as they chose to add. (Applause.) He would not quarrel with the Government if they gave them a decent minimum, provided it was a decent minimum. Referring to the ' resolution, Mr. Matthews said the clause with regard to the time limit was essential. No Government had any moral right to hand over what was the gift of the people for one year to the absolute monopoly of the brewer. (Applause.) It had given a free gift of • enormous importance, representing a large amount of wealth, into the keeping of the brewers, and they were the last people in the world to whom anything ought to be given. (Applause.) They had far too much already and took more than that to which they were entitled. Mr. Balfour said in the House of Commons in 1904 that " Our ancestors would have been wise never to have allowed this monopoly value to grow up and we ought to do our best to prevent it growing up in the future." Then why in all creation, didn't he prevent it himself? (Applause.) He had the power and the means and the men. Referring to the second part of the resolution he suggested that the magistrates knew best what the locality required. He could not understand why Mr. Balfour in his wisdom should have ventured to curtail the power of the magistrates. It was because he had very little faith in the people and less faith in the bench of men who were beginnir'es to I show their reforming zeal. Mr. Balfour destroyed the I London School Board for .the same reason that he

_ destroyed the power of the local bench. The local licensing bench was the only authority which stood between the public and the brewer, and that authority he chose to rob of its power. Alluding to the last clause of the resolution Mr. Matthews said he welcomed it because it was the extension of local self-govern- ment. They only asked that the same opportunities enjoyed by the landowner should be extended to the electorate. They would not have had the Brooklands Hotel in Lovely-lane if the voice of the people had been heard, and they would not have the licence in Gorsey-lane if the people in that locality would bestir themselves, and make themselves heard. He hoped the local bench would refuse the transfer of the Bridge Inn. If they touched the trade's interests they were often met with the cry of " Rob the poor man of his beer." He (Mr. Matthews) would rob the working man of his beer if he had the opportunity. He did not con- tend if the demands of the most rabid teetotaller were satisfied, that the millenium would begin, but he thought they would be making a hole in the inebriety of the people. They would be touching the fringe of the great question of the unemployed and the time would not be far distant when the workingman realising his self respect, would take more interest in the affairs of the country and rise to the seriousness of the advantages which he poasessed. The REV. HARVEY COOK, in seconding, said they could not make people sober by Act of Parliament, but they could give the people the power to decide whether they would have fatal or safe facilities. They urged the right of the people to the veto. It was for them to say whether they would have a public-house in their I district or not. It was as unsocial of the teetotaller to take away by force what the people wanted, as it was 1 for the brewers to force upon the people what they did I not want. For the trade to cry out that they wanted Ito damage a legitimate business, was one of those I bogey's arising out of their distorted imagination. ITemperance reformers wanted to appeal to Cesar, but they wanted Czesar to be sober. They wanted no unfair advantage, nor would they submit to any. it Was because they felt that at present the conditions were not just or equitable that they protested. They submitted 1 that the charter of the people had never had its right 1 acknowledgment by the trade they demanded that night. 1 (Applause.)

CANON HICKS' SPEBCH. The Rev. CANON Hfcxs, who had a cordial reception, said that if he differed with previous speakers at all, it was because one of them spoke somewhat slightingly of the value of such resolutions as the one which had been submitted. A good Christian was always an optimist, full of hope. He (the speaker) was sure they would never get a Government to do right unless they had plebty of good resolutions and he regarded such resolu- tions and meetings as one of the most powerful forces in our social and political life. They lay at the very root of British freedom and self-government. Let them go on agitating. (Hear, hear.) Every good man,every good citizen was an agitator. He (Canon Hicks) was always agitating. (Laughter.) It was the breath of moral freedom. To leave off agitating was to consent to social abuses, to acquiesce in political and national wrongs. He was so far an optimist that he wanted to call their recollection to the fact that they had MANY GOOD FRIENDS in the present Cabinet. There was Mr. Lewis Harcourt. (Applause.) He was the good son of a good father— (applause)—and he (Canon Hicks) did not think he would show up amiss when he had to consider in the House of Commons a Bill which he (Canon Hicks) hoped and believed the late Sir William Harcourt would have approved. Then they had at the head of the legal element in the Cabinet the Lord Chancellor and there I was no man in the Kingdom who understood the social, moral and legal aspects of the question better than he ' did, or who would be able to lay those considerations more forcibly or with more personal and social weight. He (Canon Hicks) ryas full of hope but he was not at

our question, because it is wonderful what nice sub- scriptions come round from the brewers. (Laughter.) In Warrington I have no experience whatever; but I am speaking of Manchester, Salford, Stockport, and towns thereabouts, and I know it makes an enormous difference to the action of a teetotal parson, if he has a brewery which belongs to his denomination in his neigh- bourhood. What does this mean ? It means that the interests of the people, their happiness, their morality, their progress, are being bought and sold. (Hear, bear.) It is necessary for those of us who have something of a clear insight into the movement of affairs and are willing to make a sacrifice of time and sometimes of position, to come and stand by the side of the people." (Applause.) Referring to local veto, Canon Hicks said it was not at all a dangerous or wild sugges- tion. There were thousands of parishes and villages in this muntry where there were no public-houses and there were whole areas in great towns which were with- out public-houses. This was due to the wise foresight of landlords and they asked that Parliament should con- cede to the community the same power to do without the liquor traffic as was possessed by benevolent and far-sighted landlords. (Applause.) Men who were in favour of the liquor trade said the people would never use the power. Well, if they would not use it, why make such a tremendous hullaboloo about it? (Laughter.) He believed there were many localities that would go wrong and not vote for doing away with the liquor at first, but they might see their mistake in time. He believed in the educative power of respon- sibility. (Applause.) Canon Hicks instanced the case of Port Sunlight which was started without a public. house, but afterwards the Public-House Trust Company obtained permission by the votes of the inhabitants to build one. The house,however,did no business because the people did not want anything of the kind. He believed that those places where they had not a Lever, where they lived in the slums and were being destroyed by the liquor trade, agitators should be able to go amongst the people and say: "Itis in your own power if only you will vote by a majority to do without the public- house and start a garden city down in the slums." (Applause.) He had such faith in his kind that he believed good would come of that power if it were given to them. In Canada from ocean to ocean local veto was in being and Canon Hicks gave instances of its good results. If it was good enough for Canada, why should not we have a chance ? Surely the problem of drink was acute in Great Britain. We were sighing and groaning under this heavy bondage. Why not use this marvellous power which was, after all, the power of liberty and was on the lines of constitutional freedom? There was a Property and Liberty Defence League going about and saying that temperance reformers were destroyers of liberty. There was a passage in the poet that said : "Licence they mean when they call liberty." (Applanse.) Canon Hicks also showed how the veto had succeeded in the United Statee,prohibition being in force in a number of States. In conclnsion Canon Hicks said: There is

A GREAT TORAL UPHINAVAL going on right through the world. The Far East is in unrest. The people are wanting more liberty, more progress, more enlightenment, and I am confident that there is a great moral and intellectual upheaval taking place in Western Europe. One of the great signs of the presence of the Spirit of God in our land is the determination I can see everywhere that we shall do something to purify and uplift our social and national life. We are not content with the mean housing of our poor. We are not content with the miserable failure of our Poor Law. We are not content with the slum as it is to-day. We are determined the child life of our nation shall be safeguarded in every way as it never has been before. We want progress, enlightenment, purity, and above all we want happy homes for our people. We are confident that we cannot take many steps towards these great ' ends, which are the great ends of national existence, unless the Government by wise laws gives us, the , democracy of England, greater power to push back • from us this great, polluting temptation. But if that , is done we may make steps forward, and repeated steps forward, to the consummation of our hope which is a purer, a more enlightened and a happier England for the days that are to come. (Applause.) ) The resolution was then put to the meeting and carried unanimously. MR. SLOAN'S SPEECH.

Mr. T. H. SLOAN, M.P., moved a vote of thanks to the chairman for presiding and also that Mr. Dodds be requested to forward copies of the first resolution to the Prime Minister, Chancellor of the Exchequer,Home Secretary and the Member for the Borough. As an individual who had during his Parliamentary career never seen the advisability of giving up principle for party, of sacrificing conviction on the ground of expediency, he commended the forwarding of such , resolutions. It was well to give the Prime Minister to understand that although this Government bad been two years in office and bad met with very little defeat, the country was still looking with great anxiety and anticipation to the promises made when they were in opposition. It was well to give the Chancellor of the Exchequer to understand that in so far as temperance sentiment was concerned, it had not been reduced one iota and if the Licensing Bill did not contain the reforms which were promised by every Cabinet Minister before he was appointed, were espoused on the public platform when the Govern- ment was in opposition and had since been declared, their political speeches must have come to a very low I ebb indeed. It was not sufficient for the Government to say they were sympathetic to their programme. Temperance reformers said : " Hang your sympathy ; give us legislation" They could not stop preaching temperance while the traffic was in their midst. He hoped the Licensing Bill would be a good one and that when it came into the light of dey,temperance reformers would not have been "had." They wanted a

div.head: Examiner, Saturday, February 22, 1908.
div.p: The Examiner, Saturday, February 22, 1908.

all hopeful unless they went on agitating. They owed a great deal to the mar,istrates, and if Mr. Balfour had allowed them they woad have owed a great deal more, but he was sure the justices depended very largely upon the popular approval. They wanted to know what really I was the mind of the people and if the popular mind was expressed they would be unable to act upon the Bench in defiance of the wishes of the people. (Applause.) " Why are we agitating ?" continued the speaker. I " Because we are not fairly treated by the law. Our toes are pinched and we feel it. We have felt it a long time. In the great conflict that the democracy of Eng- land are engaged in against the allurements of the liquor trade, we say the democracy has not a feir advantage. The people are weak and the liquor trade is strong. It

pawnshop, and no doctor—(laughter.)The people were in fact,living in an earthly paradise and none of them were sick and weary and sore-distressed for want of the great artificial spirit. (Laughter.) The Government would forfeit the confidence of the country if they did not deal honestly and drastically with the licensing question. If the tradesaid"Our trade is our politics"they who had an interest in this Christian country so far as social reform and the betterment of the people were concerned had a right to say "Our politics must he our principles and our principles must be our politios."(Applause.)They were not doing an injustice to the trade. Their sole desire was to make the nation sober and as far as possible to remove the temptation from the working classes. His politics perhaps would not agree with those of most of the individuals present, but he would like to

div.head: STRONG IN ITS ENORMOUS WEALTH
div.p: STRONG IN ITS ENORMOUS WEALTH

and in its great social and political influence. It is strong because on the whole the laws of the land, as they stand at present, do protect the trade and make it easy for the trade to safeguard its privileges. The people are weak and almost defenceless against it. We want to remedy that wrong. (Applause.) We say we believe the people of England are more self-controlled than they were ; that they are more sober than they were, and that on the whole the consumption of drink is going down and so is the value of brewery shares. There is an improvement on the whole in the condition , of all classes and in particular of the working classes, but we want to go faster and when we see the democracy improving in intelligence, in the power of it co-operation and in its social habits and sense of the ' decencies of life, then is the time to step in and say Is the law giving the democracy a fair chance in its endeavour to live a better and more wholesome life?' We find it is not and we want to redress the wrong. One of the most difficult questions of the present day is for us to maintain the popular rights against the enormous power of wealth. If I had time I could prove to you that almost all great wars in modern days I are manipulated by a handful of capitalists. The policy ! of nations for peace and war, and for other things too, has been too much in the hands of the great capitalists. (Applause.) We do not mind the capitalists, God bless them. I don't mind them; I am not one myself— (laughter)—but we want the people to have a chance and when you find a great dangerous trade in the hands of enormous capitalists, like the distilling and brewing trades, there is a danger to popular liberty and social progress, and we find that that trade is able somehow to

div.head: MANIPULATE ALL KINDS OF PEOPLE.
div.p: MANIPULATE ALL KINDS OF PEOPLE.

A newspaper is always in danger if it goes against the trade. Advertisements are valuable, and if you won't give advertisements to the liquor trade it is extraordinary how much money you lose. I have known other professional classes who are largely influenced by the liquor trade. I have had doctors of my acquaintance who have been good teetotallers, but they have been very shy of becoming, like me, common agitators, and for very good and obvius reasons. I have known even parsons, who are superior to most temptations—(laughter)—obliged to exercise a very great and grave professional reserve in

WARRINGTON v WIGAN.

The first of the two League matches with Wigan has resulted according to expectations, and I hope that the second will also. Warrington made a determined effort at Wigan on Saturday, but the home side were a bit better and managed to win by the comfortable margin of 11 points to 5. This result settles the West Lancashire League championship and Wigan may now be considered holders of the Cup which has rested with Runcorn since last season. Warrington would have had an excellent chance if they could have captured even one point at Wigan, but with a weakened team they were hardly expected to perform the feat.

Miss Edith Woods gave evidence bearing out this statement. She said she had had a long experience in teaching both for the Cheshire and Lancashire County Councils. When she communicated with the accountant of the County Council about her account he wrote advising her to cash the cheque for £5 4s 11d.; and make out a detailed claim of the balance due. She snbsequently received a letter from the Clerk to the Runcorn Administrative sub-Committee, who stated that he had been in cocumnnication with Mr. Rose, and he replied to the effect that Kiss Woods was told that if she extended het time and increased the staff, she did so on her own responsibility. Until the Runcorn authority's decision was ascertained she had no authority to do either. Mr. Rose also informed him that upon receiving the sub-committee's resolntion he wrote to Miss Woods stating that tha extension of time was to be allowed, the teacher's fee to be increased to 9s. for the two hours, but that the assistant was not allowed. She did not receive such a letter from Mr. Rose, and was never told by him that she was acting I on her own responsibility. Mr. Westbrook submitted that Mr. Rose was simply acting as an agent of the County Council, and was therefore not liable.

The score in the Wigan match does not accurately represent the game. Warrington had as much of the garre as the homesters and contributed the best passing displays. In fact it was only through the forwards being beaten again that the team did not come near winning. They were by no means confident of the result in Wigan and if the Warrington front rankers had displayed anything like their best form, the result might have been different. The lighter Wigan men seemed in better condition, and aided by David's unique putting-in they got possession almost continuously. Two of the tries were from forward rushes, and all Wigan's points were obtained before the interval. Warrington did better in the second half and in addition to Brooks landing a goal, both he and Isherwood had hard luck is not getting tries.

- His Honour said that if a man chose to represent that he was an agent having an authority to make a contract, and it turned out he had no such authority he was liable. He held there was a prima facie case against the defendant. . . _

- Miss J. L. Wood said she assisted her sister at the class from January Bth to March 23rd. Mr. Rose saw her several times and spoke to her. Mr Westbrook submitted that defendant was not liable for any agreement entered into merely in his representative capacity. but only if he knowingly exceeded his authority. It was not likely that Mr. Rose with his experience would have allowed Miss Woods to engage her sister unless he was empowered by the committee to do so, -

The best man on the Warrington side was undoubtedly Brooks, who played a sterling game right through and was well supported by Isherwood. Lloyd was very weak, particularly in tackling, and Fish did nothing after scoring a try in the first half. He could have made plenty of play on the left had be wished and been fit, but his tactics in the second half merely aroused the derision of the crowd. On the other wing Watkin was starved for want of opportunity, Dickenson playing a very selfish game in the centre. So far the young three-quarter has never had a chance of showing what he could do in first-class company. The only one of the Warrington forwards to distinguish himself was F. G. Jenkins, who played a splendid game and saved at least one try by his speed and determination. If the others would play with his keenness Warrington would have few defeats to chronicle.

Frederick Rose, the defenduit, was then called and said he forwarded Miss Woods' letter of the 21st December, asking for an extension of time and an assistant, to the Runcorn administrative sub-committee and they replied on February Bth, stating that the extension of time was allowed with payment at the rate of 95, for the two hours, but that the assistant was not allowed. Before that reply was received the classes had been resumed. He knew Miss Woods was then giving an extra hour and told her she was doing so entirely "on her own "as there was no authority from Runcorn. He did not, however,knovv she had engaged an assistant. On receiving the committee's reply he wrote to Miss Woods and subsequently he verbally informed her at the school of the authority's decision. William E. Hough, acting deputy clerk to the Runcorn Administrative sub-committee, said Mr. RO9O was employed as correspondent by the Cheshire County Council and anything done by him would have to be submitted to the Council through the administrative sub-committee.

Wigan were best represented by David, T. Thomas, and Sharrock. The international half back made some smart moves, but he evaded the rules a good deal by his method of putting the ball in. Referee Renton penalised him a time or two, but the Welshman per- sisted in a policy that gave his forwards possession nearly every time. If he is given the same latitude at Wilderspool to-day there will be trouble before •` time." I believe Mr. Renton will again referee the match, SO he will have opportunities of making amends, or at lmy rate keeping the tricky Welshman to the N.U. rules.

Miss Woods was re-called and admitted that when the classes were resumed after Christmas defendant told her he„had received no reply from the Runcorn Com- mittee. He, however, said she was to go on. His Honour said that if a gentleman made a contract or altered one without authority he was responsible, because it was his own doing. It struck him there must have been some misapprehension on the part of the County Council or some of the sub-committees, other- wise this line of conduct would not have been taken. He was certain Miss Woods honestly did the work she was employed to do under a contract made with Mr. Mr. Hose and it was a pitiful thing that this work should not be paid for. He need not pause to say who was to blame, but he said it was a pity that work honestly done should not be honestly paid for. " Now " said his Honour, "We come to the tardy reply of the Council, the miserable, tardy reply of the Bth February. It is not business to postpone replying to a letter of the 21st December until Bth February, especially as Christmas intervened. It is a most unbusinesslike transaction. There comes that reply in which in a niggardly spirit they, attempt to cut down the terms to which 2.1 r. Rose had assented. Mr. Rose said he did tell Miss Woods that the Council had objected in certain respects. Miss Woods absolutely denies that and I believe her tale. So it stands this way: Mr. Rose without authority made this alteration of the contract. His principals did not approve of what he had done and therefore he is personally responsible. I give judgment for the plaintiff for the amount claimed with costs."

The duel between Warrington and Wigan will be resumed to-day at Wilderspool when ,tha home club should avenge the defeat of last week. Unfortunately the side will not be any nearer full strength, though there should be no weakness apparent anywhere but at half-back. Here Lloyd cannot be expected to equal the performances of men like Lees and Jenkins. The two latter are expected to be fit again soon. Jenkins hopes to appear against Halifax, and Lees in about a fsrtnight. Taylor is at work again, and he also should be available next week.

The Warrington team for to-day is: -TiAey, full back; Fish, Isherwood, Dickenson and Watkin, three- quarters ; Lloyd and Brooks, half-backs ; Thomas, Slaugars, Belton, Jenkins, Harmer and Naylor for wards.

The most important match of the " A "team's pro- gramme was the one htst Saturday, and 'unfortunately they failed to beat their great rivals from Wigan. The home side was 'disorganised through injuries, but the same might be said for Wigan. however, the latter proved to have much the better reserves and quite outplayed the locals though the score at the end of a very keen game was only 13-10 in favour of the visitors. The Warrington men showed a strange want of confidence, and apart from the work of Jordan, Daintith and Forster there was nothing to enthuse about. Wigan were very smart and deserved at least two more tries. Kenyon seems to have quite lost his form, though he never could play a centre game. To-day's match at Wig in does not, fortunately for Warrington, count in the Combination as it is a postponed engagement, the points having already been divided. I hoped to have been able to give the posi- tions of the clubs to-day,but the Combination Secretary has not yet supplied m. with the records.

-- The "A. " team will be : C. Ashton, full back ; Tinkler, Forster, Johnson and Jordan, threequarters ; Burns and Daintith, half backs ; Kettle, Morley, Heath, Fairhurst, Holbrook and Lunt forwards. The new half bade, Burns, is a Cumberland lad from whom much is hoped. Hs is only 23 years old and weighs El stones. Let us hope he is a budding Lomas ! Johnson is a local player who has appeared before.

div.head: SECONDARY SCHOOL SCHOOL CONCERT. •
div.p: SECONDARY SCHOOL SCHOOL CONCERT. •

The pupils at the Warrington Secondary School gave their third annual concert in the Parr Hall on Thursday evening, and an interesting programme afforded con- siderable enjoyment to the large audience which assembled. There was a chorus and orchestra of 200 performers, and the manner in which they acquitted themselves testified to the excellence of the training they had received. The first part of the programme was arranged by Miss B. Dawson, Miss E. Wilkinson, Mr. R. H..Albery, Mr. J. B. Baxter, and Mr. A. E. Hoyle. It opened with a pleasing fantasia "Jack Ashore," of which a spirited rendering was given by the orchestra. Later they played " True Love Gavotte " very tastefully. The school choir did justice to the part songs " Soldier's Chorus" from " Faust," awl " Mis y Blodau," which were interpreted with precision, and a recall was accorded for the first item. Violet Brown received a hearty encore for the delightful way in which she sang "A song of April." A popular feature was the song and chorus" nikado's song"in which a number of scholars figured in costume. Roy Rice as the Mikado and Dorothy McNeil as Katisha gained high honours and the audience was so delighted that a repetition had to be given. Mary Bamforth and Ernest Parsons are deserving of special praise for their duet "Quarrelling "which was most amusing and was vigor- ously encored. The song and chorus "The ruler of the Queen's Navee " went with a capital swing, Sydney Parsonage being a successful soloist. A pretty com- position—" Two merry hearts "—was effectively inter- preted by Mary Hackett and Dorothy McNeil and the I descriptive vocal waltz" Off for the holidays" was exceptionally well presented by selected boys who engaged in sports with gusto. Needless to say these items received the cordial encores which they certainly deserved. A similar honour was accorded to John Greaves who sang "The magic montli of May" very sweetly. The songs and chorus" Roses White and roses Red,' in which Annie Taylor was the soloist, and the "Tea Sons" by Violet Brown, Mary Hackett, May Hartree and Glaeys Joynson made up a unique and entertaining item which proved a complete success. The second part of the programme, arranged by Miss E. Frost, Miss M. L. Mitchell and Miss G. M. Congdon, consisted of a scene from "Cranford "—that delightful work in which Mrs. Gaskell describes the old days in quaint Knutsford. The characters were creditably sus- tained by the following :—Miss Betty Barker, retired milliner, Ethel Cooper: Miss Matilda Jenkyns,daughter of the late rector, Ruby M. Witts ; Miss Pole, the youngest of the party,Nora Brook; Hon. Mrs. Jamieson, the ohief personage in Cranford society,Beatrice Ewan; Mrs. Forrester, widow of an officer in the army,Dorothy Collin; Peggy, Miss Barker's maid, Grace Lees.
For Bronchial Coughs take Woods' Great ePppermint Cure. 1/li, 2/9.—Advt.

div.head: APPEAL SPECIALLY TO THE WORKINGMEN
div.p: APPEAL SPECIALLY TO THE WORKINGMEN

who were the backbone of the nation. What right had ' they to agitate for shorter hours of labour if they were the means of keeping open publics houses 12 and 14 hours a day with young men and women behind the bar? (Applause.) They could not consistently say " Give us an eight hours day." What right had they to ask for the better housing of the working-classes if by their own extravagance and greed for liquor they spent ss. or GB. a week in drink and lived in a house at a rent of 3s. or 4s. ? If they wanted politicians to believe they were sincere in social reform, let them set their own house in order first. (Applause.) Let them do what they could themselves, for God helped those who helped themselves. (Applause.) Continuing Mr. Sloan said they complained against the late Government for taking away power from the licensing authorities and creating a vested interest in the traffic. If the present Government enacted a time limit of ten years it meant that compensation would not cease until the expiration of that period. It might be that in ten years the very party who created the vested interest would be in power and repeal the Liberal Government's Act and they had to run that risk. He wanted something more than a time limit and the restoration of magisterial powers which were held for three hundred years. They should have public-houses closed on election days. (Applause.) It was a foregone conclusion that the question of children entering public-houses would be dealt with. They should also have the right of vetoing the granting of a licence for any district where the people did not want it. Consideration should be given to Sunday closing and to early Saturday closing. His experience was that when public-houses closed an hour earlier on Saturday other businesses followed suit. Governments, whether Liberal or Tory, would only act in proportion to the driving power behind them. They knew some- thing about" 'driving " in Ireland—(laughter)--and he would suggest that they would do no harm by doing a bit of Cabinet-driving or House of Commons-driving. It was marvellous the effect it would have even in the least expected quarters. When the Brewers' Endow- ment Bill of 1904 was brought in he opposed it in the House of Commons and on the platform and for that he supposed he had made himself notorious for his audacity and impertinence. (Laughter.) If it was right for him to do that with a party with which he was associated and which never claimed to be a temper- ance party, it was perfectly right for him to go on the platform now whim: they had in power a party which claimed to be a temperance party, and had a huge majority to say "For goodness sake, let us have leg,isla- tion worthy of the name." (Applause.) With regard to the passing of the new Bill through the House of Lords, though the members of the Second Chamber had not to appeal to the people for their votes, he was not satisfied that they were foolish and miserable enough to ignore the will of the country even on the question of the liquor trade. " When we have done our duty" said Mr. Sloan, "I believe the House of Lords will be dealt with afterwards. (Laughter and applause.) I should think they would be, considering the things that had been said about them." (Laughter.) Mr. Sloan concluded by expressing his gratification that the clergy and ministers were now agitators on the question and said they should have been in the forefront all along the the line. (Applause.) THE BRIDGE INN LICENCE.

The Rev. JOHN YONGE seconded and at the sug- gestion of the Chairman included the speakers in the vote of thanks. He said they were always glad in Warrington to have Canon Hicks in their midst-- (applause)—and one would have been greatly gratified if a very much larger representation of clergy and ministers had been present. He hoped they would get new inspiration from the meeting, for if there was one thing in Warrington that needed new inspiration it was the cause of temperance. It had been a matter of personal regret to him for a considerable time that the old and honoured organisation known as the Warrington Temperance Association appeared to have died out. They knew that there were earnest spirits at work in the Band of Hope Union, and they were proud that a number of their British women were also very busy in the cause. (Applause.) At the same time they wanted a revival of temperance interest all -through the town, and in the churches and Sunday schools. They wanted an increase of temperance senti- ment to strengthen the hands of the magistrates to enable them to go on in the line which they began the other day at the Licensing Sessions. He hoped nothing would induce them to diverge from the decision they gave with regard to the particular application which occupied their time. Everybody who was anxious— and he supposed most Warrington people were—for the enlargement of Warrington Bridge, would be gratified if the Bridge Inn disappeared and enabled the enlarge- ment to take place, but he could not understand why a neighbourhood which had not expressed a particular desire for its presence should have the licence trans- ferred to it. He hoped the line the magistrates had taken would be adhered to faithfully to the very end. He hoped they might see in the early future a large development of the temperance spirit like they used to have twenty years ago in the town. (Applause.) Mr.E.BORELAND in supporting urged the desirability of meetings being arranged by the churches of all denominations in the district with reference to the Government Bill. None of them knew what would be in the Bill but they believed there would be nothing in it that would not be receptable to them. But for Mr. Dodds, it would not have been possible to hold the meeting. He had come to the aid of the temperance movement in Wa,ringlon at a time when he was very much needed. (Applause.) The resolution was heartily carried. In responding the CHAIRMAN said he was prepared, if the temperance friends of Warrington were willing and in earnest, to help them to develop the work they had started that night. (Applause.) If some temperance friend would convene a meeting or communicate with him so that a meeting of leading temperance workers oould be convened, they would have a Vigilance Committee because he could assure them nothing was needed more at this moment. After referring to the amount of drinking by women which, he was informed, was done at the public-house tontine clubs, Mr. Dodds said he wished to allude to the loss which the town and temperance cause had suffered in the death of their friend Mr. R. A. Naylor, one of the most generous, frank and liberal supporters of temper- ance work and of every good work in connection with the town and district. He was sure their sympathy went out to his sister and brother and he would see to it that they might know their temperance friends did not forget them in their time of trouble. Canon HICKS also returned thanks and said men like the Chairman with courage and faith were wanted in every town and not least in Warrington. (Applause).

div.head: ANCIENT SHEPHERDS. New Honorary Members.
div.p: ANCIENT SHEPHERDS. New Honorary Members.

A meeting of the Warrington District of the Loyal Order of Ancient Shepherds (A.U.) was held in the Conservative Assembly Room, Sankey-street on Tuesday evening to initiate Sir Gilbert Greenall, Bart., Coun- cillors Fulton Smith and Rogers, Mr. Robert Pierpoint, Mr. H. Hayes and Mr. J. Shaw as hon. members of the Order. After the initiation ceremony a smoking concert was held presided over by the Worthy Master, P.P.C.S. Bro. Laurence Weir. Amongst others present were : P.P.C.S.'s Peter Edgar, T. Baskerville, James Parr, T. Duckworth. Joseph Adams, P.M.'s William Lawler and G. Holford.
The toast of the " Honorary members " was proposed by the CHAIRMAN who said they felt very gratified to those gentlemen for allowing their names to be attached to the Order.

Sir GILBERT GREENALL said he felt it a great privilege to be associated with a Friendly Society, and especially with the Order of the Shepherds, which would do all in its power to help all those who were in sickness or in need. (Applause.) He pointed out how the Order also provided old-age pensions and said he believed in help- ing those who helped themselves. (Hear, hear.) Bro. ROBRRT PIERPoINT said he had been an embryo member of that society for something like twenty years. For himself he very much admired that friendly society as it helped those who suffered from sickness. (Hear, hear.) Bro.FeuroN-Smerit proposed the toast of the Warring- ton district, and spoke of the good done by friendly societies. Referring to old-age pensions, he said that in New Zealand no one was entitled to a pension unless he had contributed in some way to the welfare of his I country for twenty-five years. That was very sensible, because if that was not the case the country would be flooded with men of all nations. If the great scheme of old-age pensions was carried out in England that course which the New Zealand Government had adopted would no doubt be followed in England. He wished them every sucoess, and hoped that the membership would go on increasing. (Hear, hear, and applause.) Bro. PETER EDGAR in responding to the toast said so far as the Order and its management were concerned it was in very capable hands. The Order was of Lanca- shire birth for it was founded in Ashton-under-Lyne in 1526 by twelve men, and now it had extended across the seas to America, Africa and other countries. A.s regarded the Warrington district, he was pleased to say their position was very satisfactory, which they hoped to maintain. A vote of thanks to the Chairman and artistes was then passed. During the evening songs were provided by Messrs. A. Greenough, H. Carter, J. Shaw, G. Ratoliff and violin solos by Mr. Bradford Barton, whilst Mr. W. T. Pearce accompanied.

div.p: •_ REAL TEMPERANCE REFORM MEASURE,

which would cheer the hearts of those who had been in the wilderness on the question for many years. (Applause.) He knew of no social question that united all classes and conditions of people like the temperance cause. Mr. Sloan gave an instance of a town of 3,000 inhabitants in Ireland where prohibition was in force, and said there was no publichouse, no policeman, no

fashion. There had been one blot on the record in the shape of a dr tw at Wakefield, but all the other games were won, including clubs like Broughton Rangers, Leeds, Huddersfield, and Keigbley. After the first defeat the New Zealanders had a bad times and counting the Wigan match they had five defeats in six successive matches. The first representative game —against Yorkshire —witnessed a welcome return to form and the Tykes were beaten in hollow fashion by 23 points to 4. Three days later the tourists were at Warrington, and after a great game had to bow the knee to the Cap-holders by 8 points to 7 points. All the other representative games were lost up to the second "test," Wales, England, Lancashire and Cumberland all beating the New Zealanders, and the two latter in most decisive fashion. The first "test " saw them thrashed at Leeds by 14 points to 6 points, and it looked as if the tour was going to end most ingloriously. But at Chelsea the All Blacks redeemed themselves by a great display, and on Saturday last they startled everybody by again beating the N.U. team and thus winning the rubber. These two feats re-habilitated the reputation of the side. Personally, I never had any doubt of their quality, and in many respects I consider then superior to any teams in the Northern Union. They can teach us something in the way of combination and tactics, particularly in keeping clear of touch. It is a Northern Union —and Rugby Union too—fault in England for wing-threequarters to be bored into touch.. The All Blacks showed how this could be avoided by true centre-play and resourceful passing and re-pass- ing Altogether, the All Blacks have proved them- selves a fine team, a credit to their country and to the English race. They play an extra game at St. Helens to-day in honour of the late " Dick" Seddon, and then away to South Australia for a series of games with the newest professionals. Good luck to them !

Messenger has been the greatest scorer of the team, having kicked 57 goals, and scored 7 tries, a total of 135 points. Turtill bas played in all the matches except two, placed four goals and also accomplished a full back's rare feat of scoring a try. Smith has scored six tries, but the highest number of tries, 14„ has been credited to R. Wynyard. Rowe comes next with 11 tries, and Todd has been credited with S. Wrigley has scored 8 goals and 7 tries, and G tries have been credited to W. Wynward. That player has I had the singularly unfortunate experience of being damaged in every match he played in. Wright, the captain, has scored five tries and Johnston four.

div.head: LEAGUE.
div.p: THE LEAGUE.

Oldham still stand undefeated, notwithstanding the severe struggle on Wednesday. Most people imagined that they would suffer the fate of the All Blacks at Wigan, but they gained the day by 7 points to 3 before an excited crowd of 25,000 people from all parts of the country. G. W. Smith and L. B. Todd (of the New Zealanders) played for the winners and losers respectively. They have signed on until the end of the season. Oldham wish to maintain their unbeaten certificate, but they may fail to-day at Salford, and Wigan are keenly desirous of figuring in the first four. They also may lose to-day!

div.head: ROYAL COURT THEATRE.•
div.p: ROYAL COURT THEATRE.•
" The Village Blacksmith."

The return visit of Messrs. Dottridge, Longden and Livesey's company in the favourite play " The Village Blacksmith " has been cordially welcomed by local playgoers and large audiences have been the rule throughout the week. The play makes a powerful appeal to the sympathies of the multitude and interest never flags, in fact some of the spectators are so, carried away by the cruel wrongs perpet? wed on the, blacksmith and his wife that they give unmistakeable vent to their feelings. At the opening of the drams, John Strong, the brawny smith, is Ewen happier than the hero of Longfellow's poem, but thrlugh this villainy of Captain Leo, an athlete and rogue, his ideal home is for the time being wrecked. Husband and wife undergo great trials, but there is the populor "happy ending," the crowning scene, being Strong's triumph over Captain Leo in a realistic?: wrestling match. In the title role Mr. SAM Livesey- adds to his laurels. One could hardly imagine act actor better fitted for the part, for .he is a splendidly built, muscular man, and his portrayal is marked by fine dramatic force. Miss Maggie Edwards infuses much tenderness into her impersonation of Kate Strong, and quickly wins high favour with the audi- ence. Mr. Henry Hare as the unscrupulous Captain Leo has an unenviable part, but his portrayal does him infinite credit, and evidences histrionic talents of a high order. All the roles are in capable hands, Miss Cassie Le Grande being notably successful as Ruth Parkins, while Mr. George V. Campbell makes a, capital rustic, and is responsible for most of the, humour which relieves the story. The wrestling match between John Strong and Captain Leo with. which the play concludes is a desperate encounter, splendidly worked up, and the audience follows it with , as much enthusiasm as if it were a scene in real life.

div.p: NEXT WEEK'S PROGRAMME.

Mr. James Kiddie's popular pantomime "Dick; Whatington," will commence a six night's engagement at the theatre on Monday next, and in addition there will be a matinee on Saturday at 2 p.m. The coin' pany is one of the best that Mr. Kiddie has yet sent to Warrington, and there should be crowded houses. The pantomime has had a very successful run since its production at the Theatre It iyal, Blackburn. breaking all records at the various theatres visited. Included in the company are that well-known comedian Mr. Harry Pleon, as Idle Jack,Mr.Fred Spencer, said to be the queen of dame impersonators, as the cook the Hunnaway Bros., and Miss Flo Hilton, known as the pocket or midget edition of Vesta Tilley who wilt give four new character songs. The staging Tlcl dressing will be on an elaborate scale. The followirt week, Mr. Norman V. Norman the well-known actor, supported by Miss Beatrice Wilson is announced tcP appear in reportoire. Early in March, F. It; Benson's famous company will pay their usual annus,' visit to the Royal Court Theatre. This is the onlY occasion during the present, season on which r: rington will be favoured with a company under till-, world-renowned management, personally directekarl`" supervised by Mr. F. R. Benson.

ALL BL k.CKS TOUR COMPLETED. On Saturday last, the New Zealanders completed their tour in this country by beating the chosen of the Northern Union in the third " test at Cheltenham, thus winning the rubber. They have not had quite the successful season they anticipated from a playing sense, as the Northern Union opposition proved to be of stern stuff, and it has been a difficulty for the All Blacks, latterly, to keep a balance of wins over losses. They found the strain of playing two matches a week against professional teams in hard training rather more than they bargained for, and as a result there was not quite the same effort put into many of the mid-week matches. This undoubtedly spoiled the figures of the tour, but with the reserves much below the expected standard there was nothing else for it. Though 28 players came over, there were not more than 18 or 20 at the most who could be considered first-class aad worthy of a place in representative games.
